82882.q: According to Newton, why doesn’t the Moon fall down onto the Earth?
a: It is attached to a rope
It is carried by the wind
82882.e: Gravity pulls the Moon towards the Earth. But because it is moving sideways quickly, it circles the Earth instead of falling down.
82882.m: The Moon circles the Earth because it moves quickly.

82883.q: What did Galileo discover when he looked at the Moon through his telescope?
82883.e: Galileo saw that the Moon is not a smooth ball. It has mountains and craters like a landscape.
82883.m: The Moon has mountains and craters.

82884.q: What did Galileo say about the Earth and the Sun?
a: The Earth goes round the Sun
The Sun goes round the Earth
The Earth is a flat disc
82884.e: Galileo supported the idea that the Earth moves round the Sun. At that time many people still believed the opposite.
82884.m: The Earth goes round the Sun.

82885.q: With whom did Galileo Galilei get into serious trouble because of his ideas?
82885.e: The Church demanded that Galileo take back his teaching. After that he had to stay in his house until his death.
82885.m: Galileo got into trouble with the Church.

82886.q: From which leaning tower is Galileo said to have dropped balls?
a: From the Eiffel Tower in Paris
82886.e: According to a well-known story, Galileo dropped balls from the Leaning Tower of Pisa. Whether that really happened is not certain.
82886.m: Galileo is said to have dropped balls from the Leaning Tower of Pisa.

82887.q: What did Galileo study after watching a swinging lamp in the cathedral?
82887.e: Galileo noticed that a pendulum takes the same time for each swing. Later this was used for pendulum clocks.
82887.m: A pendulum swings in a steady rhythm.

82888.q: What did Galileo see on the Sun with his telescope?
82888.e: Galileo observed dark spots on the Sun, called sunspots. But you must never look directly at the Sun.
82888.m: There are dark sunspots on the Sun.

82889.q: What did Galileo see when he looked at the Milky Way through his telescope?
82889.e: With the naked eye the Milky Way looks like a bright band. Through the telescope Galileo saw that it is made up of countless stars.
82889.m: The Milky Way is made up of countless stars.

82890.q: Which famous painting of a smiling woman did Leonardo da Vinci paint?
82890.e: Leonardo painted the Mona Lisa. Today the painting hangs in the Louvre in Paris.
82890.m: Leonardo da Vinci painted the Mona Lisa.

82891.q: What did Leonardo da Vinci dream of, and draw machines for?
82891.e: Leonardo watched birds and drew flying machines. In his time, however, none of them was built successfully.
82891.m: Leonardo dreamed of flying like a bird.

82892.q: Which country did Leonardo da Vinci come from?
82892.e: Leonardo was born in 1452 near the village of Vinci in Italy. That is where his name comes from.
82892.m: Leonardo came from Vinci in Italy.

82893.q: What did Leonardo study closely so that he could draw people better?
82893.e: Leonardo studied the human body very closely. He drew muscles, bones and tendons.

82894.q: Which drawing by Leonardo shows a man with outstretched arms in a circle and a square?
82894.e: The Vitruvian Man shows a man inside a circle and a square. The drawing shows the proportions of the body.
82894.m: The Vitruvian Man stands in a circle and a square.

82895.q: Apart from being a painter, what else was Leonardo da Vinci?
82895.e: Leonardo was a painter, inventor, engineer and naturalist all at once. He was interested in almost everything.
82895.m: Leonardo was both a painter and an inventor.

82896.q: What do you do to milk when you pasteurise it?
a: You shake it for a long time
82896.e: When milk is pasteurised, it is heated briefly. This kills many germs and the milk lasts longer. The name comes from the scientist Louis Pasteur.
82896.m: Pasteurised milk has been heated briefly.

82897.q: Which dangerous disease did Pasteur develop a vaccine against?
82897.e: Pasteur developed a vaccine against rabies. In 1885 he used it to save a boy who had been bitten by a dog.
82897.m: Pasteur invented a vaccine against rabies.

82898.q: What did Louis Pasteur show about many diseases?
82898.e: Pasteur showed that tiny living things such as bacteria cause many diseases. Before that, many people believed bad air was to blame.

82900.q: Which famous research institute in Paris bears Pasteur’s name?
82900.e: The Pasteur Institute was founded in 1887. Scientists there still research diseases and vaccines today.
82900.m: The Pasteur Institute in Paris researches diseases.

82901.q: What did Pasteur need to be able to see bacteria?
82901.e: Bacteria are so small that you can only see them with a microscope. Pasteur worked with one a lot.
82901.m: You can only see bacteria with a microscope.

82902.q: Which drinks did Pasteur help to stop going sour or bad?
82902.e: Pasteur investigated why wine and beer go off. He found out that heating kills the harmful germs.
82902.m: Pasteur helped to make wine and beer last longer.

82903.e: Penicillin is an antibiotic. It kills bacteria or stops them from growing.

82904.q: In which year did Alexander Fleming make his famous discovery with the mould?
82904.e: In 1928 Fleming noticed that no bacteria grew around a patch of mould.

82905.q: Where was Alexander Fleming coming back from when he found the mouldy dish?
82905.e: Fleming came back from his summer holidays and found a forgotten dish with mould on it. A lucky accident!
82905.m: Fleming’s discovery was an accident after the holidays.

82906.q: What are medicines like penicillin that work against bacteria called?
82906.e: Medicines that fight bacteria are called antibiotics. Penicillin was one of the first.

82907.q: Which prize did Alexander Fleming receive in 1945?
82907.e: In 1945 Fleming received the Nobel Prize in Medicine together with two other scientists.
82907.m: Fleming received the Nobel Prize in 1945.

82908.q: Do antibiotics like penicillin help against flu caused by viruses?
a: Only if you drink a lot
82908.e: Antibiotics work against bacteria, but not against viruses. Flu is caused by viruses.
82908.m: Antibiotics do not help against viruses.

82909.q: What did penicillin later save for many people?
82909.e: Before penicillin, even small wounds could become deadly because of bacteria. The medicine saved a great many lives.

82910.q: To which continent did Maria Sibylla Merian travel to study insects?
82910.e: In 1699 Merian travelled with her daughter to Suriname in South America. There she painted tropical insects and plants.

82911.q: Which Swiss city did the family of Maria Sibylla Merian’s father come from?
82911.e: Her father Matthäus Merian was a famous copper engraver. He was born in Basel in 1593.

82912.q: In which city was Maria Sibylla Merian born?
82912.e: Maria Sibylla Merian was born in Frankfurt am Main in 1647.
82912.m: Maria Sibylla Merian was born in Frankfurt.

82913.q: What did many people in Merian’s time believe about insects?
82913.e: Back then, many people thought insects simply came from mud or rotting matter. With her pictures, Merian showed that they hatch from eggs.

82914.q: What is Maria Sibylla Merian famous for?
a: Her detailed pictures of butterflies and caterpillars
82914.e: Maria Sibylla Merian watched and painted how caterpillars turn into butterflies. Later she even appeared on the German 500 mark note.
82914.m: Merian painted caterpillars changing into butterflies.

82915.q: Which animals did Maria Sibylla Merian keep at home to watch them?
82915.e: Merian fed caterpillars with their food plants and watched how they turned into pupae. That way she could paint everything exactly.
82915.m: Merian raised caterpillars to watch them.

82916.q: In which city did Maria Sibylla Merian live before she travelled to South America?
82916.e: In 1691 Merian moved with her daughters to Amsterdam, a big trading city in Holland.

82917.q: What did Maria Sibylla Merian always paint together with the insects?
82917.e: Merian painted the insects together with the plants they feed on. That showed how animal and plant belong together.
82917.m: Merian painted insects with their food plants.

82918.q: Which country did Thomas Alva Edison come from?
82918.e: Thomas Alva Edison was born in the USA in 1847.

82919.q: Which device did Edison invent that could record sounds and play them back?
82919.e: Edison invented the phonograph in 1877. For the first time, it could record voices and play them back.

82920.q: Which invention did Edison bring into homes as a really useful light?
82920.e: Other scientists had already built light bulbs. Edison improved them so that they lasted a long time and found their way into many homes.
82920.m: Edison brought the light bulb into homes.

82921.q: Roughly how many patents did Edison have?
82921.e: In the USA, Edison registered over 1,000 inventions as patents. That is a great many.
82921.m: Edison had over a thousand patents.

82922.q: Who taught the young Edison at home for most of the time?
82922.e: Edison only went to school for a short time. After that, it was mainly his mother who taught him at home.
82922.m: Edison’s mother taught him at home.

82923.q: What nickname did Edison get because of his laboratory in Menlo Park?
82923.e: Because so many amazing inventions came out of his laboratory, people called him “the Wizard of Menlo Park”.
82923.m: Edison was called the Wizard of Menlo Park.

82924.q: What problem did Edison have with his ears?
82924.e: Edison was already hard of hearing as a young man. Even so, he worked on devices for sound.

82925.q: What did Edison need so that his light bulbs could shine in people’s homes?
a: A water wheel in the room
82925.e: In New York, Edison built one of the first power stations with an electricity network. That is how electricity got into homes.
82925.m: Light bulbs need electricity from a power network.

82926.q: What did Mary Anning search for and find on the coast?
82926.e: Mary Anning searched the cliffs for fossils, which are the remains of prehistoric animals in stone.
82926.m: Mary Anning found fossils on the coast.

82927.q: In which country did Mary Anning live?
82927.e: Mary Anning lived in the town of Lyme Regis on the south coast of England.

82928.q: Roughly how old was Mary Anning when she and her brother found an ichthyosaur skeleton?
82928.e: Mary Anning’s brother found the skull around 1811, and Mary then uncovered the skeleton. She was about 12 years old at the time.
82928.m: Mary Anning was a fossil hunter even as a child.

82929.q: Which prehistoric sea creature did Mary Anning find as the first complete skeleton?
82929.e: In 1823 Mary Anning found the first complete skeleton of a plesiosaur. It had a very long neck.
82929.m: Mary Anning found a long-necked plesiosaur.

82930.q: How did Mary Anning’s family earn a living?
82930.e: The family was poor. They sold the fossils they found to collectors and tourists.
82930.m: Mary Anning sold fossils to make a living.

82931.q: Which English tongue twister is said to be about Mary Anning?
82931.e: Many people say the tongue twister “She sells seashells by the seashore” is about Mary Anning. But this is not certain.
82931.m: A tongue twister reminds us of Mary Anning.

82932.q: Why was Mary Anning not allowed to become a member of the important society of geologists in London?
a: Because she did not speak English
Because she lived too far away
82932.e: At that time, women were not allowed to join the Geological Society. Even so, many scientists used her finds.
82932.m: As a woman, Mary Anning was not recognised for a long time.

82933.q: Why was searching for fossils on the cliffs dangerous for Mary Anning?
82933.e: The best fossils came out of the cliffs after storms. Rocks often fell down at those times. Mary Anning was once almost buried.
82933.m: Searching for fossils on cliffs can be dangerous.

82934.q: What is the name of Darwin’s famous book from 1859?
a: Journey to the Centre of the Earth
82934.e: Darwin’s book “On the Origin of Species” came out in 1859. In it he explains evolution.
82934.m: Darwin wrote the book on the origin of species.

82935.q: At which famous English university did Isaac Newton do his research?
82935.e: Newton studied and did research for many years at Trinity College, University of Cambridge.
82935.m: Newton did his research in Cambridge.

82936.q: What did Galileo see on Venus that we also know from the Moon?
a: It has phases like the Moon
It has many moons like Jupiter
It has a red spot like Jupiter
82936.e: Galileo saw that Venus sometimes looks like a crescent and sometimes almost round. This fits with the idea that it travels around the Sun.
82936.m: Venus shows phases like the Moon.

82937.q: Which flying prehistoric animal was Mary Anning the first to find in England?
82937.e: In 1828 Mary Anning found the first skeleton of a pterosaur in England. Today it is called Dimorphodon.

82938.q: What cushions knocks in the knee like a little pillow?
82938.e: The meniscus is a crescent-shaped disc of cartilage between the thighbone and the shinbone. It cushions knocks when walking and jumping.
82938.m: The meniscus cushions knocks in the knee.

82939.q: How many menisci does each knee have?
82939.e: Each knee has an inner meniscus and an outer meniscus. So together there are two.

82940.q: What are the ligaments called that cross like an X in the middle of the knee joint?
82940.e: In the knee there is a front and a back ligament that cross over each other. They stop the lower leg sliding away forwards or backwards.
82940.m: The cruciate ligaments keep the knee stable.

82941.q: What does your knee joint do when you ride a bike?
82941.e: When pedalling, the knee is bent and straightened again and again. That is why cycling is good exercise for the knees.
82941.m: When cycling, the knee bends and straightens again and again.

82942.q: What do you call legs where the knees touch but the feet are apart?
82942.e: When the knees come together inwards, the legs look like the letter X. In small children this is often normal and grows out.
82942.m: With knock knees, the knees touch.

82943.q: What do you call legs with a large gap between the knees?
82943.e: The legs then form a round shape together like the letter O. Many babies have slightly curved legs that later become straight.
82943.m: With bow legs, the knees are far apart.

82944.q: When can you turn your lower leg a little at the knee?
a: When the leg is fully straight
Never, the knee is purely a hinge
82944.e: When the knee is bent, the ligaments are a little looser, so the lower leg can turn slightly. When the leg is straight, the knee is firm and stable.
82944.m: Only with a bent knee can you turn your lower leg a little.

82945.q: How do you land after a jump in the way that is kindest to your knees?
82945.e: Bent knees cushion the impact like a spring. With stiff legs, the whole jolt goes into the joints.
82945.m: After a jump, land with slightly bent knees.

82946.q: What do people often wear after a knee injury to support the knee?
82946.e: A knee support fits tightly around the knee. It supports the joint and gives stability when walking.
82946.m: A support helps an injured knee.

82947.q: What does the doctor do when a shoulder is dislocated?
a: She puts it back in place
She sticks a plaster on it
82947.e: With a dislocated shoulder, the bone has slipped out of the joint. The doctor carefully pushes it back.
82947.m: A dislocated shoulder is put back in place.

82948.q: Which large joint pops out of its socket most often?
82948.e: The shoulder is very mobile but not as firmly built as other joints. That is why it dislocates more easily in a fall.
82948.m: Of all the large joints, the shoulder dislocates most often.

82949.q: Why can you move your shoulder so far in all directions?
a: The socket is small and flat
The socket is deep and narrow
The joint has many ligaments made of bone
The joint is a hinge joint
82949.e: The round head of the upper arm bone sits in only a small, flat socket. So it has plenty of room to move.
82949.m: The flat socket makes the shoulder very mobile.

82950.q: Which bone forms the socket of the shoulder?
82950.e: There is a small hollow on the shoulder blade. The head of the upper arm bone sits in it.
82950.m: The shoulder socket belongs to the shoulder blade.

82951.q: Which bone sits with its round head in the shoulder joint?
82951.e: The upper arm bone has a round head at the top. This head moves in the shoulder joint.
82951.m: The head of the upper arm bone sits in the shoulder joint.

82952.q: What mainly holds the upper arm bone in place in the shoulder?
82952.e: Strong muscles and tendons surround the shoulder joint. They hold the upper arm in place like a cuff.
82952.m: Muscles and tendons hold the shoulder together.

82953.q: What do you need to lift your arm up?
82953.e: Strong muscles lie over the shoulder. They pull the arm up, to the side and forwards.

82954.q: What is a good way to warm up your shoulders before sport?
82954.e: With arm circles, the shoulder joint moves in all directions. That way the muscles and joint get warm and ready for sport.
82954.m: Arm circles warm up the shoulders.

82955.q: Which joint do you mainly move when you put your hand up at school?
82955.e: When you put your hand up, you lift your whole arm above your head. This movement is done mainly by the shoulder.
82955.m: Putting your hand up mainly moves the shoulder.

82956.q: What is the hollow in the pelvis called, where the top end of the thighbone sits?
82956.e: The hip socket is a deep hollow in the pelvic bone. The head of the thighbone turns in it.
82956.m: The thighbone sits in the hip socket.

82957.q: Why can you move your leg at the hip less far than your arm at the shoulder?
a: The hip socket is very deep
The hip is made of cartilage
82957.e: The head of the thighbone sits deep in the hip socket. This makes the hip very stable but a bit less mobile.
82957.m: The deep hip socket makes the hip stable.

82958.q: What do older people sometimes get when their hip joint is badly worn?
82958.e: A worn hip joint can be very painful. Doctors can replace it with an artificial joint made of metal and plastic.
82958.m: A worn hip joint can be replaced with an artificial one.

82959.q: What does the hip joint connect?
82959.e: In the hip joint, the thighbone sits in the pelvis. That way the leg is connected to the body and can move.
82959.m: The hip joint connects the leg to the pelvis.

82960.q: Which joint do you bend when you pull your knee up high to your chest while marching?
82960.e: When the whole leg goes up forwards, the hip bends. It connects the leg to the pelvis.
82960.m: The hip bends when you lift your leg forwards.

82961.q: Which toy do you keep spinning around your tummy by circling your hips?
82961.e: With a hula hoop you move your hips quickly back and forth. That way the hoop stays up and spins around your body.
82961.m: Circling your hips keeps a hula hoop going.

82962.q: Which joints carry the weight of the whole upper body when you stand?
82962.e: The upper body rests on the pelvis. From there the weight goes through the hip joints into the legs.
82962.m: The hip joints carry the weight of the upper body.

82963.q: How many hip joints does a person have?
82963.e: Each leg is attached to the pelvis by its own hip joint. So there is a left and a right hip joint.

82964.q: How many joints does an index finger have, not counting the wrist?
82964.e: The index finger has three finger bones. Between them and at the hand there are three joints altogether.
82964.m: An index finger has three joints.

82965.q: How many finger bones does the thumb have?
82965.e: The thumb is shorter than the other fingers. It has only two finger bones; the other fingers have three.
82965.m: The thumb has two finger bones.

82966.q: Why is it harder to move your fingers when it is very cold?
a: Cold muscles and tendons get stiff
82966.e: In the cold, muscles and tendons become less supple. If you warm up your hands, your fingers can move easily again.
82966.m: Cold fingers are stiff and warm fingers move easily.

82967.q: What is the finger joint right at the front, by the fingertip, called?
82967.e: It is called the end joint because it is at the end of the finger. With it you bend only the fingertip.
82967.m: The front finger joint is called the end joint.

82968.q: What is the finger joint called where the finger joins the hand?
82968.e: This joint is at the base, that is the start, of the finger. There the finger is connected to the middle of the hand.
82968.m: Where the finger starts at the hand is the base joint.

82969.q: In which direction do the finger joints bend easily?
a: Towards the back of the hand
82969.e: The finger joints work like little hinges. They bend towards the palm, so you can make a fist.

82970.q: How do you often sprain a finger when playing ball games?
82970.e: If the ball hits the straight fingertip, a joint gets jammed. This often happens in volleyball or basketball.
82970.m: A ball hitting the fingertip can injure a finger joint.

82971.q: What are the hard bumps on the back of the hand called, which you see when you make a fist?
82971.e: When you make a fist, the base joints of the fingers stick out as bumps. They are called knuckles.
82971.m: You see your knuckles when you make a fist.

82972.q: What is the joint between the lower leg and the foot called?
82972.e: The joint of the foot is called the ankle joint. You need it to walk, run and jump.
82972.m: The joint of the foot is called the ankle joint.

82973.q: What are the two hard bumps on the left and right of the ankle called?
82973.e: At the ankle there is an inner and an outer ankle bone. They are the ends of the two lower leg bones.
82973.m: You can feel an ankle bone on the inside and outside of the ankle.

82974.q: Which ligaments of the ankle are most often injured when you go over on your ankle?
82974.e: Usually the foot turns inwards, so the outer side is overstretched. That is why the ligaments on the outside of the joint get injured.
82974.m: When you go over on your ankle, the outer ligaments usually suffer.

82975.q: What does the ankle joint do when you stand on tiptoe?
82975.e: On tiptoe, the foot points downwards. The ankle joint makes this movement together with the calf muscles.
82975.m: On tiptoe, the ankle points the foot downwards.

82976.q: Which shoes protect the ankle especially well when hiking in the mountains?
82976.e: High hiking boots reach over the ankle and give it support. That way you are less likely to go over on your ankle on stony paths.
82976.m: High hiking boots support the ankle.

82977.q: What is the thick tendon at the back above the ankle, which runs to the heel, called?
82977.e: The Achilles tendon connects the calf muscles to the heel bone. It is the strongest tendon in the body.
82977.m: The Achilles tendon runs to the heel.

82978.q: Which exercise can strengthen your ankles?
a: Lying down for a long time
82978.e: When balancing, many small muscles around the ankle work. This makes it more stable, and you are less likely to go over on it.
82978.m: Balancing on one leg strengthens the ankles.

82979.q: What helps first when your ankle swells up after you go over on it?
a: Cooling it and raising the foot
82979.e: Cold and a raised foot make the swelling less bad. Then an adult should check whether it needs a doctor.
82979.m: Cool a twisted ankle and raise it.

82980.q: Why should you not yank small children up by their hands and swing them around?
82980.e: In small children, strong pulling can make a bone at the elbow slip out of place. This hurts, and the child no longer wants to move the arm.
82980.m: Never pull small children by the arms with a jerk.

82981.q: How many bones meet in the elbow joint?
82981.e: In the elbow, the upper arm bone meets the two forearm bones, the ulna and the radius. That makes three bones.
82981.m: Three bones meet in the elbow.

82982.q: Which muscle on the back of the upper arm straightens the elbow?
82982.e: The triceps is at the back of the upper arm. When it contracts, the arm straightens at the elbow.

82983.q: Which movement does the elbow allow, apart from bending and straightening?
82983.e: In the elbow, the radius can turn around the ulna. That way you can turn your palm up or down.
82983.m: Thanks to the elbow, you can turn your forearm.

82984.q: Where does it hurt with ‘tennis elbow’?
a: On the outside of the elbow
On the sole of the foot
82984.e: With tennis elbow, tendons on the outside of the elbow are overloaded. It can also happen without tennis, for example from lots of work with a computer mouse.
82984.m: Tennis elbow hurts on the outside of the elbow.

82985.q: Apart from a helmet, which protection is important for your arms when skateboarding?
82985.e: When you fall, you often land on your elbows. Padded protectors protect the skin and the joint.
82985.m: Elbow pads protect your arms when skateboarding.

82986.q: How far can you straighten your arm at the elbow?
82986.e: You can bend and straighten your arm at the elbow until it is straight. Bending backwards is not possible; a bone stops the movement.
82986.m: The elbow only straightens the arm until it is straight.

82987.q: Which nerve causes the tingling when you knock your elbow?
82987.e: The ulnar nerve lies at the elbow directly under the skin. If it gets knocked, it tingles all the way into the little finger.
82987.m: The ulnar nerve tingles when you knock your elbow.

82988.q: What is injured in a sprain?
82988.e: In a sprain, the ligaments around a joint are overstretched. The bone is not broken.
82988.m: In a sprain, the ligaments are overstretched.

82989.q: How can you often recognise a sprain?
82989.e: After a sprain, the joint hurts and swells up. You often can hardly move it.

82990.q: What does the E stand for in the RICE rule for sports injuries?
82990.e: RICE stands for Rest, Ice, Compression and Elevation. Elevation means raising the injured part of the body above the heart so it swells less.

82991.q: What is the right way to put an ice pack on a sprained joint?
82991.e: Ice directly on the skin can damage the skin. A cloth in between protects the skin and still cools it.
82991.m: Wrap ice packs in a cloth.

82992.q: Should you carry on playing football with a freshly sprained foot?
82992.e: An injured joint needs rest, otherwise the injury gets worse. That is why you stop playing straight away.
82992.m: With a sprain, you stop playing straight away.

82993.q: Where do you most often get a sprain when running and jumping?
82993.e: When running and jumping, you easily go over on your foot. That is why the ankle is the joint most often sprained.
82993.m: The foot is the most commonly sprained.

82994.q: Why does the skin often turn blue with a sprain?
82994.e: In the injury, small blood vessels tear. The blood collects under the skin and forms a bruise.
82994.m: A bruise comes from blood under the skin.

82995.q: What helps to prevent sprains in sport?
a: Sitting still for a long time
82995.e: Warmed-up muscles and ligaments are more elastic. They hold the joint better, and you get injured less often.
82995.m: People who warm up get injured less often.

82996.q: What usually causes the cracking sound when someone cracks their knuckles?
a: A gas bubble in the joint
82996.e: When you pull on the joint, a gas bubble suddenly forms in the fluid inside it. That makes the cracking sound.
82996.m: Knuckle cracking comes from a gas bubble in the joint.

82997.q: Why can you not crack the same finger again straight away?
a: The gas first has to dissolve again
The finger has gone to sleep
82997.e: After cracking, it takes about 20 minutes for the gas to dissolve back into the joint fluid. Only then can it crack again.
82997.m: A cracked joint needs a break before it cracks again.

82998.q: When should you see a doctor about a cracking joint?
a: When it cracks in the morning
82998.e: Cracking without pain is usually harmless. But if the joint hurts or swells up, a doctor should have a look.
82998.m: Only painful joint cracking needs to be checked.

82999.q: Apart from a gas bubble, what can cause a cracking sound in a joint?
a: A tendon snapping over a bone
82999.e: Sometimes a tendon slides over a bump on a bone when you move. This can also crack or snap.
82999.m: A snapping tendon can crack too.

83000.q: A doctor cracked the knuckles of only one hand for over 50 years. What did he find?
83000.e: The doctor Donald Unger cracked only the knuckles of his left hand and then compared both hands. Neither hand developed a joint disease, and in 2009 he received a joke prize for research.
83000.m: According to what we know today, knuckle cracking does not make joints ill.

83001.q: Where do many people hear a crack when they stand up from a deep squat?
83001.e: Many people’s knees crack when bending deeply and straightening. Without pain, this is usually harmless.
83001.m: Knees often crack when you stand up from a squat.

83002.q: Who is usually more flexible: children or older people?
83002.e: In children, muscles, tendons and ligaments are still very stretchy. With age, flexibility decreases if you do not practise it.
83002.m: Children are usually more flexible than older people.

83003.q: When should you stretch during sport?
a: Straight after getting up in bed
83003.e: Warm muscles stretch better. That is why you warm up first and only stretch afterwards.
83003.m: Only stretch when your muscles are warm.

83004.q: In which sport do you perform on the floor and on apparatus such as the high bar and parallel bars?
83004.e: Artistic gymnasts need a lot of strength and great flexibility. They show their routines on the floor and on different pieces of apparatus.
83004.m: Artistic gymnastics needs a lot of strength and flexibility.

83005.q: What is it better not to do when stretching?
83005.e: Jerky bouncing can injure muscles. It is better to move slowly into the stretch and hold it calmly.

83006.q: What is the gymnastics exercise called where you stand on your hands and feet, bent backwards?
83006.e: In the bridge, the body forms a high arch. This needs a very flexible back and flexible shoulders.
83006.m: You need a flexible back for the bridge.

83007.q: What are you testing when you sit with straight legs and reach for your toes?
83007.e: The further forwards you get, the more flexible your back and the muscles at the back of your legs are. This test is often done in PE.
83007.m: Reaching for your toes shows how flexible you are.

83008.q: In which kind of exercise are there poses such as ‘downward dog’?
83008.e: Yoga is made up of many poses with animal names. They stretch the body and make it flexible.

83009.q: What do you call circus performers who can bend their bodies extremely?
83009.e: Contortionists are so flexible that they can bend almost like a snake. They practise for years to do it.

83010.q: What happens to your flexibility if you move very little for a long time?
83010.e: If muscles and joints are moved very little, they become stiffer. Regular exercise keeps you flexible.
83010.m: If you move little, you get stiffer.

83011.q: Which sea creature has no bones and can squeeze through tiny gaps?
83011.e: An octopus has no skeleton made of bones. Only its hard beak does not fit through every opening; the rest is completely soft.
83011.m: An octopus can squeeze through the tiniest gaps.

83012.q: What do you do with your chin before you do a forward roll?
83012.e: With your chin on your chest, your neck becomes rounded. That way you roll over your back instead of your head.
83012.m: In a forward roll, tuck your chin to your chest.

83013.q: What should your back be like in a forward roll?
83013.e: A round back rolls softly over the mat. A straight back would thump hard onto the floor.
83013.m: In a forward roll, make your back round.

83014.q: Where do you put your hands in a forward roll?
a: Shoulder-width apart in front of your feet
83014.e: Your hands are on the mat in front of your feet, shoulder-width apart. They brake and help you roll.
83014.m: In a forward roll, your hands are in front of your feet.

83015.q: What is the somersault forwards called in PE?
83015.e: In gymnastics, the somersault is called a forward roll. You roll forwards over your rounded back.
83015.m: In gymnastics, the somersault is called a forward roll.

83016.q: What is the gymnastics exercise called where you roll backwards over your back?
83016.e: In a backward roll, you roll backwards from a crouch. Your hands push off the floor next to your ears.
83016.m: To roll backwards, you do a backward roll.

83017.q: What do you practise forward rolls on in PE?
83017.e: A mat is soft and cushions you. That way rolling does not hurt.
83017.m: You practise forward rolls on a mat.

83018.q: What helps beginners learn a forward roll?
83018.e: On a sloping surface you roll forwards more easily by yourself. That makes the movement easier to learn.
83018.m: A sloping mat makes the forward roll easier.

83019.q: What is a flip in the air called, where your hands do not touch the ground?
83019.e: In a somersault, you turn all the way round once in the air. You land on your feet again.
83019.m: A somersault is a flip in the air.

83020.q: What do you do in the splits?
a: Spread your legs wide apart in a line
83020.e: In the splits, you sit on the floor with straight legs. The legs point in opposite directions and form a straight line.
83020.m: In the splits, your legs form a straight line.

83021.q: What are the splits called where one leg points forwards and the other backwards?
83021.e: The legs lie lengthways in the direction you are facing. That is why they are called front splits.
83021.m: In the front splits, one leg points forwards and the other backwards.

83022.q: What are the splits called where both legs point to the side?
83022.e: The legs are spread out to the left and right. This form is called the side splits and is especially hard for many people.
83022.m: In the side splits, both legs point to the side.

83023.q: In which dance do dancers often show the splits?
83023.e: Ballet needs a lot of flexibility. Splits and jumps with the legs spread wide are part of it.
83023.m: The splits are often part of ballet.

83024.q: What is the safest way to learn the splits?
83024.e: Muscles and tendons only become more stretchy slowly. If you practise a little every day, you make safe progress without injury.
83024.m: You learn the splits with patience and regular stretching.

83025.q: Which muscles are stretched when you spread your legs to the side?
a: The muscles on the inside of the thigh
The muscles on the upper arm
83025.e: When spreading your legs sideways, the muscles on the inside of the thighs pull. They have to give way so the legs can go wide apart.
83025.m: Spreading your legs stretches the inner thighs.

83026.q: Which joints have to be especially mobile for the splits?
83026.e: In the splits, the legs are spread wide at the hip joint. The more mobile the hip is, the lower you can get.
83026.m: For the splits you need mobile hips.

83028.q: What should you do if you suddenly feel a stabbing pain while practising the splits?
83028.e: A stabbing pain can mean that a muscle is injured. Then you stop straight away and take a break.
83028.m: If it stabs, stop straight away.

83029.q: What touches the ground one after another when you do a cartwheel?
83029.e: In a cartwheel, you first put down one hand and then the other. Then both feet land one after the other.
83029.m: In a cartwheel, first the hands come down and then the feet.

83030.q: What are your legs like in the air during a cartwheel?
83030.e: The straight, spread legs turn over your head. That is why a cartwheel looks like a star.
83030.m: In a cartwheel, your legs are straight and spread.

83031.q: In which direction do you move when doing a cartwheel?
a: Round in a circle on the spot
83031.e: In a cartwheel, you turn sideways over your hands. You land on the same line, but a bit further along.

83032.q: Why is the gymnastics move called a ‘cartwheel’?
a: Arms and legs turn like spokes
You need a bike for it
83032.e: Your arms and legs are stretched out wide and turn around the middle of your body. This is like the spokes of a wheel.
83032.m: In a cartwheel, arms and legs turn like spokes.

83033.q: What is a cartwheel with a quarter turn called, where you land on both feet at the same time?
83033.e: In a round-off, you turn at the end and land with your legs together. You then face the direction you came from.
83033.m: In a round-off, you land on both feet at the same time.

83034.q: Which parts of the body briefly carry your whole weight when doing a cartwheel?
83034.e: When your legs are in the air, you are supported only on your hands. That is why you need strength in your arms and shoulders.
83034.m: In a cartwheel, your arms briefly carry your whole body.

83035.q: What helps when practising so that your cartwheel is nice and straight?
83035.e: Your hands and feet should land on the same straight line. A line on the floor helps you keep the direction.
83035.m: A line on the floor helps with a straight cartwheel.

83036.q: Where are your arms when you take a run-up for a cartwheel?
a: Folded in front of your tummy
83036.e: At the start you stretch your arms up high. That way you can swing forwards onto your hands.
83036.m: For a cartwheel, first stretch your arms up high.

83037.q: How can you make a cartwheel harder once you are good at it?
83037.e: If you can do a cartwheel safely, you practise it with only one hand on the floor. This needs even more strength and balance.

a: A bar that turns around a point
83038.e: A lever is a rigid bar that rests on one spot and turns there. With it you can move heavy things using less force.
83038.m: A lever is a bar that turns around a point.

83039.q: What is the point a lever turns around called?
83039.e: Every lever rests on a point or is fixed there. It moves around this pivot.

83040.q: Where do you push on a long lever so that it is easiest?
a: As far from the pivot as possible
As close to the pivot as possible
83040.e: The further from the pivot you push, the less force you need. But you have to move the lever a longer way.
83040.m: Far from the pivot you need the least force.

83041.q: You want to lift a heavy stone with a long bar. What do you put under the bar, close to the stone?
83041.e: The solid block is the pivot. The bar turns around it, and you can lift the stone with little force.
83041.m: A lever needs a firm pivot.

83042.q: A child weighing 20 kg sits 2 m from the middle of the seesaw. Where must a child weighing 40 kg sit so that the seesaw balances?
83042.e: The second child is twice as heavy, so it only needs half the distance. 20 kg times 2 m makes 40, and 40 kg times 1 m also makes 40.
83042.m: A child twice as heavy sits half as far from the middle.

83043.q: With which spanner is a very tight nut easiest to undo?
83043.e: A long spanner is a long lever. You need less force on it to turn the nut.
83043.m: A long spanner undoes tight nuts more easily.

83045.q: Which part of a rowing boat works like a lever?
83045.e: The oar turns in a holder on the boat. The rower pulls on the handle, and the blade pushes against the water.

83046.q: What does a building crane need at its back end so that it does not tip over?
83046.e: The arm of the crane is like a big lever. Heavy concrete blocks on the other side keep it balanced.
83046.m: A counterweight stops the crane from tipping over.

83047.q: What do you need a crowbar for?
a: To lift or prise open heavy things
83047.e: With a crowbar you can lift heavy things a little or prise something firm open. It works as a lever.
83047.m: With a crowbar you lever heavy things up.

83048.q: What material is a crowbar usually made of?
83048.e: A crowbar has to withstand very large forces without bending. That is why it is made of hard steel.
83048.m: A crowbar is made of steel.

83049.q: What is the slot at the bent end of many crowbars for?
a: For hanging it on your belt
83049.e: You push the nail head into the slot and press the bar down. Then the lever pulls the nail out of the wood.
83049.m: With the slot of a crowbar you pull out nails.

83050.q: What is another name for a crowbar?
83050.e: Crowbar and wrecking bar are two names for the same tool. It is a bar of iron or steel for prising things open.
83050.m: A crowbar is also called a wrecking bar.

83051.q: Why is a crowbar quite long?
a: So that you need less force
83051.e: A long lever needs less force than a short one. That is why you can move even heavy things with a long crowbar.
83051.m: The longer the crowbar, the less force you need.

83052.q: What can you put under a crowbar so that it has a firm pivot?
83052.e: The block of wood is hard and does not give way. The bar can move on it as on a pivot.
83052.m: A hard block serves as the crowbar's pivot.

83053.q: Who often opens jammed doors with a crowbar in an emergency?
83053.e: The fire brigade sometimes has to get into a house or a car quickly. With crowbars and other tools they open jammed doors.
83053.m: The fire brigade carries crowbars for emergencies.

83054.q: Which way does the load move when you push the long end of a crowbar down?
83054.e: The crowbar turns around the pivot like a seesaw. When one end goes down, the other end with the load rises.
83054.m: When you push the long arm down, the load rises.

83055.q: What do you open with a bottle opener?
a: The metal cap of a bottle
The cork of a wine bottle
83055.e: A bottle opener lifts the metal cap with the jagged edge, the crown cap, off the bottle. For corks you need a corkscrew.
83055.m: With a bottle opener you lift off metal caps.

83056.q: In which century was the metal cap with a jagged edge for glass bottles invented?
83056.e: William Painter from the USA was granted a patent for this cap in 1892. That was in the 19th century.
83056.m: The jagged bottle cap is over 130 years old.

83057.q: Which tool that many children in Switzerland know often has a bottle opener built in?
83057.e: A Swiss pocket knife has many tools in one. It often includes a small bottle opener.
83057.m: A pocket knife often has a bottle opener.

83059.q: Which simple machine is in a bottle opener?
83059.e: The opener presses on the cap and pulls on the edge at the same time. With little force on the handle, you lever the cap off.
83059.m: A bottle opener is a lever.

83060.q: Where does the hook of a bottle opener grip the cap?
a: Under the edge of the cap
In the middle of the cap
At the bottom of the bottle
83060.e: The hook slides under the jagged edge. From there it levers the cap upwards.
83060.m: The hook grips under the edge of the cap.

83061.q: Why is a bottle opener with a long handle easier to use?
a: The long handle needs less force
83061.e: The handle is the effort arm of the lever. The longer it is, the less force you have to use.
83061.m: A long handle makes opening easier.

83062.q: Why does a metal cap hold so tightly on the bottle without an opener?
a: Its edge is pressed around the neck of the bottle
83062.e: In the factory, the jagged edge is pressed firmly around the neck of the bottle. So the bottle stays sealed.
83062.m: The cap is pressed firmly around the neck of the bottle.

83063.q: Where is the pivot of a pair of scissors?
a: At the screw in the middle
At the cutting edge at the front
83063.e: The two parts of the scissors are joined in the middle by a screw or rivet. They turn there.
83063.m: Scissors turn around the screw in the middle.

83064.q: Where do scissors cut thick cardboard most easily?
a: Right at the front at the tips
83064.e: Close to the pivot, the force of your hand acts most strongly on the material. At the tips you need much more force.
83064.m: You cut thick cardboard close to the pivot.

83065.q: How many blades does a pair of scissors have?
83065.e: A pair of scissors has two blades with handles. They turn around the screw in the middle and cut together.

83066.q: Why do garden shears for thick branches have long handles?
a: So that you have more force
So that they do not rust
83066.e: Long handles are long lever arms. With them you can cut through even thick branches.
83066.m: Long handles give scissors more force.

83067.q: Which scissors are safest for young children?
83067.e: Rounded tips do not stab. So children are less likely to hurt themselves when doing crafts.

83068.q: How do you pass a pair of scissors to someone safely?
a: By throwing them through the air
83068.e: If you hand over the scissors closed and handle first, you cannot stab anyone. The other person can take them easily by the handle.
83068.m: Pass scissors closed and handle first.

83069.q: What happens if the screw of a pair of scissors is too loose?
a: The paper gets stuck between the blades
83069.e: With a loose screw, the blades no longer lie close together. The paper slips between them and is not cut cleanly.
83069.m: With a loose screw, scissors cut badly.

83070.q: What is different about real left-handed scissors compared with normal scissors?
83070.e: On left-handed scissors, the top blade is on the other side. So when cutting with your left hand you can see the cutting line, and the blades press together properly.

83071.q: Why do pliers have long handles and short jaws?
a: So that the jaws grip very tightly
So that they do not rust
83071.e: The long handles are long lever arms. That is why the short jaws at the front squeeze with great force.
83071.m: Long handles give pliers a lot of force.

83072.q: What are the front parts of pliers that grip called?
83072.e: The two front parts are called the jaws of the pliers. They grip or cut the material.

83073.q: Which pliers do you use to pull nails out of wood?
83073.e: Pincers have sharp, rounded jaws. You grip the nail with them and lever it out.
83073.m: You pull out nails with pincers.

83074.q: Which pliers do you use to cut through thin wire?
83074.e: Side cutters have sharp cutting edges on the side. With them you can easily snip through wire.
83074.m: You cut wire with side cutters.

83075.q: Why do pliers for electricians have thick plastic handles?
a: So that they are more colourful
So that they rust more easily
83075.e: Plastic does not conduct electricity. The thick handles protect your hands if you touch a live cable.

83076.q: Where do you hold pliers to have the most force?
a: At the ends of the handles
In the middle of the jaws
83076.e: At the ends of the handles you are furthest from the pivot. That is where the lever force is strongest.
83076.m: Right at the back of the handles you have the most force.

83077.q: What does the dentist use to pull out a tooth that cannot be saved?
83077.e: The dentist has special forceps for teeth. With them she grips the tooth firmly and loosens it.
83077.m: Teeth are pulled out with forceps.

83078.q: Where do you put a hard nut in the nutcracker so that it cracks easily?
83078.e: Close to the joint, the nutcracker presses with the greatest force. Further forward you would need much more force.
83078.m: Put the nut close to the joint.

83079.q: Why can you crack a nut more easily with a nutcracker than with your hand?
83079.e: The long handles of the nutcracker are levers. With a little force on the handles, a lot of force acts on the nut.
83079.m: A nutcracker multiplies the force of your hand.

83080.q: Which nut do you often crack with a nutcracker?
83080.e: Hazelnuts have a hard shell and fit well in the nutcracker. Coconuts are too big, and you open peanuts with your fingers.
83080.m: Hazelnuts are cracked with a nutcracker.

83081.q: What does a well-known wooden nutcracker often look like?
a: Like a soldier or a king
83081.e: The colourful wooden nutcrackers are usually painted as soldiers or kings. You put the nut in their mouth and push the lever on their back down.
83081.m: Wooden nutcrackers often look like soldiers.

83082.e: The Russian composer Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky wrote the music. The ballet was first performed in 1892.
83082.m: The ballet “The Nutcracker” is by Tchaikovsky.

83083.q: At what time of year is the ballet “The Nutcracker” often performed?
83083.e: The story takes place on a Christmas Eve. That is why many theatres show the ballet in December.
83083.m: “The Nutcracker” is a ballet for Christmas time.

83085.q: Which bird of the Swiss mountain forests cracks Swiss stone pine nuts and hides them as a winter store?
83085.e: The spotted nutcracker opens the stone pine cones with its strong beak. Forgotten hiding places help new stone pines to grow.
83085.m: The spotted nutcracker hides stone pine nuts for the winter.

83086.q: What is the grooved wheel called that a rope runs over on a crane?
83086.e: A pulley is a wheel that turns, with a groove around its edge. A rope runs in the groove without slipping off.
83086.m: A pulley is a wheel that a rope runs over.

83087.q: What does a fixed pulley at the top of a scaffold do?
a: It changes the direction of the force
83087.e: With a fixed pulley you pull down and the load goes up. This is more comfortable because you can use your own weight.
83087.m: A fixed pulley changes the direction of the force.

83088.q: How much force do you save with a single fixed pulley?
83088.e: With a fixed pulley you have to pull just as hard as the load is heavy. It only makes pulling more comfortable.
83088.m: A fixed pulley saves no force.

83089.q: How do you raise the Swiss flag on a flagpole?
a: You pull down on the rope at the bottom
You climb up with the flag
83089.e: There is a pulley fixed at the top of the pole. When you pull the rope at the bottom, the flag goes up on the other side.
83089.m: On a flagpole, a pulley helps raise the flag.

83090.q: Roughly how much force do you need with a movable pulley that moves with the load?
83090.e: With a movable pulley, two sections of rope carry the load. That is why you only have to pull about half as hard.
83090.m: A movable pulley halves the force needed.

83091.q: What does the cable of a chairlift run over on the pylons?
83091.e: There are many pulleys on top of the pylons. The cable runs over them and can move with almost no friction.
83091.m: The cable of a chairlift runs over pulleys.

83092.q: What often hangs over an old draw well so that you can pull up the bucket more easily?
83092.e: The rope runs over the pulley and down to the bucket. You pull on the other end, and the bucket comes up.
83092.m: A pulley helps pull the bucket out of the well.

83093.q: What does the steel cable on the arm of a building crane run over?
83093.e: There are pulleys on the arm and on the hook. The cable runs over them and lifts the heavy loads.
83093.m: The cable of a crane runs over pulleys.

83094.q: In a block and tackle, which pulleys move up together with the load?
83094.e: The movable pulleys hang from the load and rise with it. The fixed pulleys stay at the top on the ceiling or on a beam.
83094.m: Movable pulleys rise with the load.

83095.q: A load hangs from 4 supporting sections of rope in a block and tackle. Roughly how much force do you need?
83095.e: The load is shared between four sections of rope. That is why you only need about a quarter of the force.
83095.m: With four supporting sections of rope you need a quarter of the force.

83096.q: A crate weighs 90 kg and hangs from 3 supporting sections of rope. Roughly how much force do you need?
83096.e: Three sections of rope share the load. 90 kg divided by 3 makes 30 kg.
83096.m: The more sections of rope carry the load, the less force you need.

83097.q: In a block and tackle with 4 supporting sections of rope, you pull 4 m of rope. How high does the load rise?
83097.e: Each of the four sections of rope gets shorter as the load rises. 4 m divided by 4 makes 1 m.
83097.m: The load rises much less far than the length of rope you pull.

83098.q: What are blocks and tackles used for on a sailing ship?
a: To pump water out of the boat
83098.e: Sails are big and heavy, and the wind pushes against them. With blocks and tackles, the sailors can still hoist them.
83098.m: On sailing ships, blocks and tackles help with the sails.

83100.q: What can you use to pull a bike up to the ceiling in the garage easily?
83100.e: A block and tackle on the ceiling makes pulling up easy. So the bike hangs in the air, saving space.
83100.m: With a block and tackle you can pull a bike up easily.

83101.q: Why do many entrances have a ramp?
a: So that you can run faster
83101.e: You cannot get up stairs on wheels. On a ramp you can push a wheelchair or pushchair up easily.

83102.q: Up which ramp do you push a heavy cart with the least force?
83102.e: The gentler the ramp, the less force you need. But the way is longer.
83102.m: A gentle ramp needs little force.

83103.q: What is a ramp called in physics?
83103.e: A ramp is a sloping surface. In physics it is called an inclined plane and is one of the simple machines.
83103.m: A ramp is an inclined plane.

83104.q: What do removal workers often push heavy furniture up onto a lorry?
83104.e: On a sloping ramp you can push heavy furniture up on wheels. That needs much less force than lifting.
83104.m: A ramp helps when moving house.

83105.q: How did the ancient Egyptians probably get heavy stones up when building the pyramids?
83105.e: Researchers think the Egyptians built ramps of mud and stones. They pulled the stone blocks up on them.
83105.m: The Egyptians probably built ramps for their pyramids.

83106.q: What is a U-shaped ramp for skateboarders called?
83106.e: A half-pipe looks like a pipe cut in half. Skaters ride back and forth in it and jump up at the edge.

83107.q: Where does a marble roll down faster?
83107.e: The steeper the ramp, the more strongly gravity pulls the marble down. That is why it gets faster.
83107.m: On a steep ramp the marble rolls faster.

83108.q: How do you get a boat on its trailer into the water at the lakeside?
a: You roll it down a sloping ramp
You carry it down some stairs
You drop it from a bridge
You pull it over a ladder
83108.e: On the shore there are sloping ramps that lead into the water. You slowly roll the boat down them on its trailer.
83108.m: Boats are rolled into the water down a ramp.

83109.q: What does a wedge look like?
a: A block that tapers to a point at the front
83109.e: A wedge is thick on one side and thin and pointed on the other. With the pointed side it pushes into material.
83109.m: A wedge tapers to a point at the front.

83110.q: Which kitchen tool works like a wedge?
83110.e: The blade of a knife is very thin at the edge. Like a wedge, it pushes the food apart.
83110.m: A knife cuts like a wedge.

83111.q: What do you push under a door to keep it open?
83111.e: The doorstop wedge jams between the floor and the door. So the door cannot swing shut.
83111.m: A doorstop wedge keeps the door open.

83112.q: Why does a sharp wedge go into wood more easily than a blunt one?
83112.e: With a narrow point, all the force presses on a small spot. That is why the wood gives way more easily.
83112.m: A sharp edge goes in more easily.

83113.q: Which teeth work like a wedge when you bite something off?
a: The baby teeth at the back
83113.e: The incisors at the front are flat and sharp. Like a wedge they split an apple, for example.
83113.m: The incisors bite like a wedge.

83114.q: Why is a nail pointed at the end?
a: It pushes the wood apart like a wedge
So that it does not rust
83114.e: The point pushes the wood fibres aside. So you can hammer the nail into the wood.
83114.m: The point of a nail works like a wedge.

83115.q: Why is a ship pointed at the front?
a: So that the ship looks nicer
So that fish get out of the way
So that the ship is heavier
83115.e: The pointed shape at the front works like a wedge in the water. So the ship can move forward more easily.
83115.m: A pointed ship parts the water.

83116.q: What did stonemasons in the past use to split large blocks of stone?
83116.e: They hammered several wedges into a row of holes in the stone. The wedges pushed the stone apart so hard that it split.

83117.q: What separates the teeth of a zip in the slider when you open it?
83117.e: There is a small wedge inside the slider. When you pull the slider down, it pushes the teeth apart.
83117.m: In a zip, a small wedge separates the teeth.

83118.q: Which way do you turn a normal screw to screw it in?
83118.e: Most screws have a right-hand thread. You turn them clockwise to screw them in and the other way to take them out.

83119.q: What is the part you screw onto a threaded bolt called?
83119.e: The nut also has a thread inside. You screw it onto the bolt so that two parts hold firmly together.
83119.m: You screw a nut onto a bolt.

83120.q: What can an Archimedes' screw move upwards?
83120.e: A large screw turns inside a sloping tube. As it does, water is pushed upwards bit by bit.

83121.q: Which device turns like a screw into the cork of a bottle?
83121.e: The corkscrew has a spiral-shaped point. You twist it into the cork and then pull it out.
83121.m: A corkscrew turns into the cork like a screw.

83122.q: Why does a screw usually hold more firmly in wood than a nail?
83122.e: The threads of the screw dig into the wood. That is why it cannot simply be pulled out.
83122.m: Screws hold more firmly than nails.

83123.q: How do you adjust the height of many piano stools?
83123.e: There is a large screw under the seat. When you turn the seat, it screws up or down.
83123.m: On a piano stool you turn the seat to change the height.

83124.q: What is a screw with a cross in its head called?
83124.e: The head of this screw has two slots that form a cross. You need a matching screwdriver for it.
83124.m: A screw with a cross is called a cross-head screw.

83125.q: What is the axle of a wheel?
a: The rod that the wheel turns around
83125.e: The axle sits in the middle of the wheel. The wheel turns around it.
83125.m: A wheel turns around its axle.

83126.q: Why is the steering wheel of a bus very big?
a: So that it is easier to turn
So that it takes up more room
So that the bus goes faster
83126.e: The bigger the wheel, the less force you need to turn the axle. So a big steering wheel is easier to move.
83126.m: A big steering wheel is easier to turn.

83127.q: On an old coffee grinder, what do you use to turn the grinding mechanism?
83127.e: The crank is a handle on a long arm. When you turn it in a circle, the axle with the grinding mechanism turns.

83128.q: How many axles does a normal car have?
83128.e: A car has a front axle and a rear axle. There are two wheels on each axle.
83128.m: A normal car has two axles.

83129.q: What do you put on a squeaky axle so that it turns more easily?
83129.e: Oil reduces the friction between the wheel and the axle. Then nothing squeaks any more, and the wheel turns more easily.
83129.m: Oil makes an axle turn smoothly.

83130.q: What drives the waterwheel at an old mill?
83130.e: The water flows onto the paddles of the wheel and turns it. Through the axle, the grinding mechanism is then driven.
83130.m: A waterwheel is turned by flowing water.

83131.q: What is the middle part of a bike wheel called, which the axle goes through?
83131.e: The hub sits in the middle of the wheel. The spokes go out from it to the rim.
83131.m: The axle of a bike wheel goes through the hub.

83132.q: Why does the rim of a wheel move faster than a spot near the axle?
a: It travels a longer distance in one turn
83132.e: With each turn the rim makes a big circle, the middle only a small one. So in the same time the rim covers more distance.
83132.m: The rim of a wheel is faster than its middle.

83133.q: What does an astronaut put on for a trip outside the space station?
83133.e: Outside in space there is no air to breathe. The spacesuit protects the astronaut and gives them air.
83133.m: Outside in space you need a spacesuit.

83134.q: What does an astronaut in a spacesuit get to breathe?
83134.e: The backpack of the spacesuit holds a supply of oxygen. So the astronaut can breathe, even though there is no air outside.
83134.m: The spacesuit gives the astronaut oxygen.

83135.q: What colour are the spacesuits for trips outside the space station usually?
83135.e: White reflects the glaring sunlight. That way the suit does not get too hot in the sun.
83135.m: Spacesuits for outside are usually white.

83136.q: Why does the helmet of a spacesuit have a golden visor?
83136.e: In space sunlight is very glaring and dangerous for the eyes. The thin layer of gold blocks some of it, a bit like sunglasses.
83136.m: The golden visor protects the eyes from glaring sunlight.

83137.q: What is in the large backpack of a spacesuit?
83137.e: The backpack is like a small life-support system. It provides air and electricity and keeps the astronaut cool.
83137.m: The backpack on the spacesuit supplies the astronaut with air and electricity.

83138.q: How heavy is a spacesuit for trips into space when you weigh it on Earth?
83138.e: A spacesuit like this weighs well over 100 kilograms on Earth. But in space the astronaut does not feel this weight.
83138.m: A spacesuit for outside is very heavy on Earth.

83139.q: What does an astronaut wear under the spacesuit so as not to get too hot?
83139.e: Thin tubes are sewn into this underwear. Cool water flows through them and cools the body.
83139.m: Cool water in tubes cools the astronaut in the spacesuit.

83140.q: What does an astronaut wear in the rocket at launch?
83140.e: During launch and landing, astronauts wear a spacesuit. It protects them if air escapes from the capsule.
83140.m: Astronauts wear a spacesuit at launch.

83141.q: What happens to a pen that you let go of in the space station?
83141.e: In the space station you are weightless. That is why nothing falls down; everything floats.
83141.m: When you are weightless, everything floats.

83142.q: What is it called when astronauts float in the space station?
83142.e: The space station is constantly falling around the Earth. That is why the astronauts do not feel their weight and float.
83142.m: Floating in space is called weightlessness.

83143.q: What shape does a drop of water take when it is weightless?
83143.e: Without weight, water pulls itself together into a round ball. These water balls float through the space station.
83143.m: In space water forms floating balls.

83144.q: What happens to an astronaut's back in space?
83144.e: Without weight, the bones of the spine no longer press so hard on each other. That is why the astronaut gets a few centimetres taller in space.
83144.m: In space you get a little taller.

83145.q: Why do astronauts in space have to do sport every day?
a: So that their muscles stay strong
So that they do not freeze
83145.e: When you are weightless, muscles and bones need almost no strength. Without daily training they would become weak.
83145.m: Sport keeps muscles and bones strong in space.

83146.q: What do astronauts have to do with tools in the space station?
83146.e: Otherwise loose tools would float away. That is why astronauts fasten everything with Velcro, straps or cords.
83146.m: In space you fasten everything so that it does not float away.

83147.q: How do astronauts move around in the space station?
83147.e: Because they float, they cannot walk. They push themselves off handles with their hands and feet.
83147.m: In the space station you float from handle to handle.

83148.q: Where in the space station is there an up and a down?
83148.e: When you are weightless, nothing pulls you down. That is why you can work on the ceiling just as well as on the floor.
83148.m: When you are weightless, there is no real up and down.

83149.q: What is astronauts' food often packed in?
83149.e: Pouches and tins hold the food in place and keep it fresh for a long time. Open food would float away when you are weightless.
83149.m: Astronaut food is usually well packed.

83150.q: What do astronauts often eat instead of bread?
83150.e: Bread makes lots of crumbs. These would float around and could get into eyes or equipment.
83150.m: Astronauts eat tortillas because bread makes crumbs.

83151.q: What do you add to dried astronaut food before you eat it?
83151.e: A lot of astronaut food is dried so that it is light and keeps for a long time. With water it becomes soft and edible again.
83151.m: You make dried food edible again with water.

83152.q: How is salt provided for astronauts in the space station?
83152.e: Loose grains of salt would float away. That is why the salt is dissolved in a liquid and dripped on.
83152.m: In space salt is liquid so that it does not float away.

83153.q: What do astronauts drink from in space?
a: From a pouch with a straw
From a cup without a lid
83153.e: From an open glass, the water would float out as balls. With a straw they suck it out of the pouch.
83153.m: In space you drink from a pouch with a straw.

83154.q: How does food taste to many astronauts in space?
83154.e: In space, fluid rises into the head and the nose is often blocked, like with a cold. That is why they taste less.
83154.m: In space food tastes less strong to many people.

83155.q: How does fresh fruit get to the space station?
a: From a tree in the station
83155.e: Cargo spacecraft regularly bring supplies to the space station. Sometimes there is fresh fruit too.
83155.m: Fresh fruit comes into space with the supply flight.

83156.q: Why are crumbs dangerous in the space station?
a: They float into eyes and equipment
They make stains on the floor
83156.e: In space crumbs do not fall to the floor. They float around and can irritate eyes or disturb equipment.
83156.m: Crumbs float around in space and cause trouble.

83157.q: What do astronauts sleep in on the space station?
83157.e: Each astronaut has a small sleeping cabin. There they sleep in a sleeping bag.
83157.m: Astronauts sleep in a sleeping bag.

83158.q: Why is the sleeping bag fastened to the wall?
a: So that it does not float around
83158.e: When weightless, a sleeping astronaut would drift through the station. That is why the sleeping bag is fastened down.
83158.m: The sleeping bag is fastened so that you do not float away.

83159.q: How many times a day do astronauts on the space station see the Sun rise?
83159.e: The space station goes once around the Earth in about an hour and a half. So the astronauts see around 16 sunrises a day.
83159.m: On the space station the Sun rises many times a day.

83160.q: What do astronauts often wear over their eyes when they sleep?
83160.e: In the station lamps are shining, and the Sun often shines through the windows. A sleep mask makes it dark.
83160.m: A sleep mask helps you fall asleep in space.

83161.q: What do your arms often do when you sleep while weightless?
83161.e: Without weight, your arms do not fall down. That is why many astronauts tuck their arms into the sleeping bag.
83161.m: In space your arms float forwards while you sleep.

83162.q: Why do some astronauts wear earplugs when they sleep?
83162.e: In the space station, fans and machines are always running. Earplugs help against the humming.
83162.m: The equipment in the space station is always humming.

83163.q: Roughly how many hours a night do astronauts sleep on the space station?
83163.e: People need enough sleep in space too. About 8 hours of sleep are planned in the daily schedule.

83164.q: What is the small room called where an astronaut sleeps on the space station?
83164.e: The sleeping cabin is about the size of a phone box. There each astronaut has a little peace and quiet.
83164.m: Each astronaut has a small sleeping cabin.

83165.e: On a spacewalk, an astronaut in a spacesuit climbs out of the spacecraft. Outside they repair or build something.
83165.m: On a spacewalk you go outside the spacecraft.

83166.q: What is an astronaut attached to the space station with during a spacewalk?
83166.e: Without being secured, the astronaut could drift off into space. That is why they are attached to strong tethers.
83166.m: On a spacewalk you are always well secured.

83168.q: Why do astronauts go on a spacewalk?
83168.e: On the outside of the space station, equipment has to be installed or repaired. That can only be done outside.
83168.m: Outside in space, astronauts repair equipment.

83169.q: How long does a spacewalk often last today?
83169.e: Work outside is slow and tiring. A trip out of the space station often lasts several hours.
83169.m: A spacewalk often lasts many hours.

83170.q: Through which room does an astronaut leave the space station?
83170.e: In the airlock, the air is pumped out before the outer door opens. That way no air escapes from the station.
83170.m: You go out into space through an airlock.

83171.q: How many astronauts usually go outside together on a spacewalk?
83171.e: Usually two astronauts work outside together. That way they can help each other.
83171.m: On a spacewalk two astronauts usually work together.

83172.q: What do astronauts have to hold on to especially well when working outside in space?
83172.e: A tool that you let go of drifts away. That is why the tools are also secured with small tethers.
83172.m: Outside in space you secure your tools too.

83173.q: What is Claude Nicollier's mother tongue?
83173.e: Claude Nicollier comes from the French-speaking part of Switzerland. People speak French there.
83173.m: Claude Nicollier comes from French-speaking Switzerland.

83174.q: In which spacecraft did Claude Nicollier fly into space?
83174.e: The Space Shuttle was a spacecraft that could land like an aeroplane. Nicollier made all his flights in it.
83174.m: Claude Nicollier flew in the Space Shuttle.

83175.q: How many times did Claude Nicollier fly into space?
83175.e: Claude Nicollier flew into space in 1992, 1993, 1996 and 1999. That makes four flights.
83175.m: Claude Nicollier flew into space four times.

83176.q: In which town on Lake Geneva was Claude Nicollier born?
83176.e: Claude Nicollier was born in 1944 in Vevey in the canton of Vaud. Vevey lies on Lake Geneva.
83176.m: Claude Nicollier comes from Vevey on Lake Geneva.

83177.q: What did Claude Nicollier do in 1999 as the first Swiss person?
83177.e: On his last flight he climbed out of the Space Shuttle. Outside he worked on the Hubble Telescope.
83177.m: Claude Nicollier was the first Swiss person to go outside in space.

83178.q: What was Claude Nicollier's job before he became an astronaut?
83178.e: Claude Nicollier was a pilot in the Swiss Air Force. He had also studied physics and astronomy.
83178.m: Before going into space, Claude Nicollier was a pilot.

83179.q: How does the toilet on the space station work?
a: With air that sucks everything away
With sand like a cat litter tray
83179.e: Without gravity, nothing falls down. That is why a stream of air sucks everything away, a bit like a vacuum cleaner.
83179.m: The toilet in space sucks everything away with air.

83180.q: What is made from the astronauts' urine on the space station?
83180.e: A machine cleans the urine very thoroughly. Afterwards it is clean drinking water again.
83180.m: On the space station urine is turned back into drinking water.

83181.q: What do astronauts hold on to on the toilet?
83181.e: Otherwise they would float away from the toilet. That is why there are handles and loops for the feet.
83181.m: On the toilet in space you hold on tight.

83182.q: What do astronauts often wear at launch because they cannot go to the toilet for a long time?
83182.e: During launch and landing, the astronauts sit strapped in for hours. That is why they wear a special nappy.
83182.m: Astronauts wear a nappy at launch.

83183.q: What has to be running on the space toilet before you use it?
83183.e: Only when the suction is running is everything safely pulled into the container. Otherwise something would float around.
83183.m: The space toilet only works with the suction running.

83184.q: What happens to the solid waste from the space station toilet?
a: It later burns up in the atmosphere
It is flushed down to Earth
It stays in the station for ever
83184.e: The waste goes into a cargo spacecraft. This later burns up when it enters the Earth's atmosphere.
83184.m: Waste from the space station burns up in the atmosphere.

83185.q: What is the dog Laika famous for?
a: She was the first animal to orbit the Earth
She was the first dog to land on the Moon
She found a stone from space
83185.e: Laika was the first living creature to fly in an orbit around the Earth. Before that, only short flights into space had been possible.
83185.m: Laika was the first living creature to orbit the Earth.

83186.q: Which country sent Laika into space?
83186.e: The Soviet Union was a large state that included Russia. At that time it was very successful in space travel.
83186.m: The Soviet Union sent Laika into space.

83187.q: Where did Laika live before she was chosen?
83187.e: Laika was a stray dog from Moscow. People thought such dogs could cope well with cold and hunger.
83187.m: Laika used to be a stray dog.

83188.q: Which satellite did Laika fly into space in?
83188.e: Sputnik 2 was a Soviet satellite. It had a small cabin for Laika.

83189.q: Did Laika come back to Earth alive?
83189.e: A return was not yet possible at that time. Laika died just a few hours after launch because it got too hot in the capsule.
83189.m: Laika did not come back to Earth.

83190.q: Which animals flew into space in 1960 and came back healthy?
83190.e: The dogs Belka and Strelka circled the Earth for a day. Then they landed safe and sound. The dog Laika had already flown in 1957 and did not return.
83190.m: Belka and Strelka came back from space healthy.

83191.e: In a countdown you count backwards, for example 3, 2, 1, 0. At zero the rocket launches.
83191.m: In a countdown you count backwards to zero.

83192.q: What happens at a rocket launch when the countdown reaches zero?
83192.e: The countdown shows exactly when it starts. At zero the rocket lifts off.
83192.m: At zero the rocket lifts off.

83193.q: Which number comes after 4 in a countdown?
83193.e: In a countdown you count backwards. So after 4 comes 3.
83193.m: In a countdown each number gets smaller.

83194.q: Which language does the word “countdown” come from?
83194.e: Countdown is an English word: you count down to zero.

83195.q: Where did the idea of the countdown before a rocket launch come from?
83195.e: In the German film “Woman in the Moon” from 1929, people counted backwards before a rocket launch. Later, space travel took over this idea.
83195.m: The idea of the countdown for rocket launches comes from an old film.

83196.q: When is there often a countdown with lots of people in Switzerland?
a: At midnight on New Year's Eve
In the afternoon at snack time
83196.e: Just before midnight on New Year's Eve, lots of people count backwards together. At zero the new year begins.
83196.m: On New Year's Eve lots of people count backwards together.

83197.q: What can happen if a problem is found before the launch?
83197.e: Safety comes first. If there is a problem, the countdown is stopped and everything is checked carefully.
83197.m: If there is a problem, the countdown is stopped.

83198.q: Which number is the very last one in a countdown?
83198.e: A countdown always ends at zero. Then the moment everyone has been waiting for has come.

83199.e: The astronauts sit in the space capsule during the flight into space. It sits on top of the rocket.
83199.m: Astronauts travel into space in a space capsule.

83200.q: Where is the space capsule at launch?
a: Right at the top of the rocket
Right at the bottom by the engines
Next to the rocket on the ground
83200.e: The capsule is at the top, and the big fuel tanks and engines are at the bottom. That way the astronauts can be taken away quickly if there is danger.
83200.m: The space capsule sits on top of the rocket.

83201.q: What is the Russian space capsule called that astronauts fly to the space station in?
83201.e: The Soyuz capsule has been flying for many decades. Very many astronauts have already flown to the space station in it.
83201.m: Soyuz is a Russian space capsule.

83202.q: In which space capsule did astronauts fly to the Moon in 1969?
83202.e: With Apollo 11, astronauts flew to the Moon in 1969. Two of them walked on the surface of the Moon.
83202.m: People flew to the Moon in Apollo.

83203.q: How much room do astronauts have in a space capsule?
a: As much as in a sports hall
As much as in a house
As much as in a stadium
83203.e: A space capsule is cramped, roughly like a small car. The astronauts sit close together.
83203.m: It is cramped in a space capsule.

83204.q: What protects the space capsule from the great heat on the way back?
83204.e: When it enters the atmosphere, the outside of the capsule gets very hot. The heat shield on the underside protects the astronauts.
83204.m: The heat shield protects the capsule from the heat.

83205.q: What is it called when a space capsule attaches itself to the space station?
83205.e: The capsule moves very slowly up to the space station. Then it attaches itself there, which is called docking.
83205.m: Space capsules dock at the space station.

83206.q: What is the space capsule for astronauts from the company SpaceX called?
83206.e: Since 2020 astronauts have flown to the space station in the Crew Dragon capsule.
83206.m: Crew Dragon takes astronauts to the space station.

83207.q: What slows down a space capsule just before landing?
83207.e: Large parachutes open and slow the capsule down. That way it lands gently.
83207.m: Parachutes slow down the space capsule.

83208.q: Where did the American space capsules land after the flight to the Moon?
83208.e: The American Moon capsules landed in the sea with parachutes. Ships then picked up the astronauts.
83208.m: The Moon capsules landed in the sea.

83209.q: Where does the Russian space capsule usually land when it brings astronauts back from the space station?
83209.e: The Russian capsule lands on solid ground on a flat steppe in Kazakhstan. Just before it reaches the ground, small braking rockets fire.
83209.m: The Russian space capsule usually lands in Kazakhstan.

83210.q: What fires on the Russian space capsule just before it hits the ground?
83210.e: Just above the ground, small rockets fire. They slow the capsule down strongly once more.
83210.m: Braking rockets make the landing softer.

83211.q: What happens to the outside of the capsule when it enters the atmosphere?
83211.e: The capsule is very fast and hits the air with great force. That makes it extremely hot on the outside.
83211.m: On the way back the capsule gets very hot on the outside.

83212.q: Why can astronauts often not walk properly straight after landing?
a: Because their body has got used to floating
Because they have eaten too much
Because the ground is too hot
83212.e: After a long time in space, the body is used to being weightless. It needs a few days to get used to its weight again.
83212.m: After space, the body has to get used to walking again.

83213.q: Who picks up the astronauts after a landing in the sea?
83213.e: Rescue teams wait nearby with a ship. They bring the capsule and the astronauts on board.
83213.m: After a landing in the sea, a ship picks up the capsule.

83214.q: What is the landing of a space capsule in water called?
83214.e: When a capsule lands in the sea, it is called a splashdown. Today's American capsules land like this too.
83214.m: A landing in water is called a splashdown.

83215.q: Where do astronauts practise spacewalks on Earth?
83215.e: Under water you float almost like in space. That is why astronauts practise in spacesuits in large tanks.
83215.m: Astronauts practise floating in a water tank.
