85036.e: The front part of a boat is called the bow. It is often pointed so that it cuts through the water well.
85036.m: The front of a boat is the bow.

85037.q: What were people's first boats often made of?
85037.e: Long ago, people hollowed out thick tree trunks. Boats like this are called dugout canoes.
85037.m: The first boats were often wooden dugouts.

85038.q: Why does a rubber dinghy float?
85038.e: A rubber dinghy is blown up and full of air. That makes it very light, so it floats well.
85038.m: A rubber dinghy floats because it is full of air.

85039.q: Why do you wear a life jacket on a boat?
a: So you stay on top of the water
So you do not get cold
85039.e: A life jacket gives extra buoyancy in water. If you fall in, it keeps you at the surface.
85039.m: A life jacket keeps you up in the water.

85040.q: What colour are life jackets often?
85040.e: Bright colours are easy to see on the water. That way rescuers can find a person quickly.

85041.q: What are many life jackets filled with?
85041.e: Foam is very light and contains lots of tiny air bubbles. That is why it floats well and carries the person.
85041.m: Many life jackets contain light foam.

85042.q: When is the best time to put on a life jacket?
a: Before you get into the boat
Only once you are in the water
Only when the sun is shining
85042.e: It is very hard to put on a life jacket in the water. So you put it on before getting in.
85042.m: You put on the life jacket before the trip.

85043.q: How should a life jacket fit?
a: Well fastened and the right size
85043.e: A jacket that is too big or open can slide up in the water. It must be fastened and fit well.
85043.m: A life jacket must fit well and be fastened.

85044.q: In which water sport do people usually wear a life jacket?
85044.e: In a canoe you can easily capsize. The life jacket then keeps you at the surface.
85044.m: You wear a life jacket when canoeing.

85045.q: Why do life jackets often have a collar behind the head?
a: It keeps the head above water
85045.e: The collar is also filled with foam. It helps keep the mouth and nose above the water.
85045.m: The collar of the jacket supports the head.

85046.q: Apart from a life jacket, what else is needed for a safe boat trip with children?
85046.e: Even with a life jacket, children on the water need an adult watching them. The jacket does not replace supervision.
85046.m: Children on the water always need supervision.

85047.q: What happens to a fresh raw egg in a glass of tap water?
85047.e: A fresh egg is heavier than the same amount of tap water. That is why it lies at the bottom of the glass.
85047.m: A fresh egg sinks in tap water.

85048.q: What do you have to add to water to make a fresh egg float?
85048.e: If you dissolve lots of salt in the water, the water holds the egg up. Stirring with a spoon helps the salt dissolve.
85048.m: An egg floats in very salty water.

85049.q: Why does an egg float in salt water but not in tap water?
a: Salt water is heavier than tap water
The egg gets lighter in salt water
85049.e: The same amount of salt water weighs more than tap water. That is why salt water pushes up more strongly.
85049.m: Salt water holds things up better than fresh water.

85050.q: Where can you float especially easily because the water is very salty?
85050.e: The Dead Sea is extremely salty. That is why people float on the surface there almost like a cork.
85050.m: You float very easily in the Dead Sea.

85051.q: What does an old egg often do in a glass of tap water?
85051.e: More air has collected inside an old egg. That is why it stands up in the water or even floats.
85051.m: An old egg rises in water.

85052.e: Seawater has lots of salt dissolved in it. That is why it tastes salty and you cannot drink it.

85053.q: Where is it easier to swim: in the sea or in a lake?
85053.e: Seawater is salty and so holds you up better. In a freshwater lake you float a little lower.
85053.m: You swim more easily in the salty sea.

85054.q: What happens to the egg in salt water if you pour in lots of tap water?
85054.e: Adding more tap water makes the salt water weaker. Then it no longer holds the egg up, and it sinks.
85054.m: Diluted salt water no longer holds the egg up.

85055.q: What does a block of wood do if you push it under water and let go?
85055.e: Buoyancy pushes the light wood upwards. When you let go, it comes quickly to the surface.
85055.m: Wood rises in water when you let go.

85056.q: Is there wood that sinks in water?
85056.e: Most kinds of wood float. But some very heavy woods, such as ebony, sink in water.

85057.q: Which wood is especially light and is used for model aeroplanes?
85057.e: Balsa is one of the lightest woods. It floats very well and is easy to cut.

85058.q: How does a wooden board lie in the water?
a: Part of it is under water
It lies fully on top without dipping in
It stands upright in the air
85058.e: Even floating wood dips a little way into the water. Only part of the board sticks out of the water.
85058.m: Floating wood dips in a little way.

85059.q: Why were tree trunks often transported on rivers in the past?
a: Because wood gets lighter in water
85059.e: Wood floats, so the logs were left to drift down the river or tied together into rafts. This is called timber rafting.
85059.m: In the past, logs were floated down rivers.

85060.q: What happens to a branch that lies in water for years?
a: It can soak up water and sink
85060.e: Over time, wood can soak up water. Then it gets heavier and can go under.

85061.q: Which of these toys floats in the bath?
85061.e: A wooden toy boat is lighter than the same amount of water. That is why it floats.

85062.q: Which floats better: a thin wooden stick or an iron nail of the same size?
85062.e: Wood is much lighter than iron of the same size. The wooden stick floats, the iron nail sinks.

85063.q: What does an ordinary pebble do in water?
85063.e: A pebble is heavier than the same amount of water. That is why it goes under.

85064.q: Which stone is so light that it floats on water?
85064.e: Pumice forms from lava and is full of air holes. That is why it can float.

85065.q: What is it called when you throw a flat stone so that it bounces several times across the water?
85065.e: You throw a flat stone fast and low across the water. It bounces several times before it sinks. In Switzerland people also call it “schiferen”.
85065.m: A stone thrown flat can bounce across the water.

85066.q: What appears on the water when you throw a stone in?
85066.e: The stone pushes the water away as it goes in. Waves form and spread out in circles.
85066.m: A stone in water makes circular waves.

85067.q: What do you usually hear when a stone falls into water?
85067.e: The stone throws up water and makes a splashing sound. Big stones make a louder “splosh”.
85067.m: A stone falls into the water with a splash.

85068.q: Why are there lots of stones on the bottom of a stream?
a: Because stones get lighter in water
85068.e: Stones are heavier than the same amount of water, so they sink to the bottom. There they stay, even when water flows over them.
85068.m: Stones sink to the bottom of the stream.

85069.q: Why are pebbles in a stream often round and smooth?
a: The water rolls and grinds them for a long time
85069.e: The flowing water rolls the stones against each other for many years. This grinds off the corners and the stones become round.

85070.q: Can a stone float on a wooden board in water?
a: Yes, if the board can carry it
85070.e: If the stone lies on a big board, the floating wood carries it along. If the stone is too heavy, everything sinks.
85070.m: A board can carry a small stone.

a: You throw it to people in the water
You wear it as a hat
You roll it along the road
85071.e: A lifebuoy is thrown to a person in the water. They hold on to it and stay afloat.
85071.m: A lifebuoy helps people in trouble in the water.

85072.e: Lifebuoys are brightly coloured. That way you can spot them quickly on the water.
85072.m: Lifebuoys are coloured to be easy to see.

85073.q: Where in Switzerland do you often find lifebuoys?
a: On lake shores and on boats
85073.e: Lifebuoys hang ready on many lake shores, in harbours and on boats. So people can help quickly in an emergency.
85073.m: Lifebuoys hang on shores and on boats.

85074.q: Why is a rope often attached to a lifebuoy?
a: So you can pull the person to the shore
So you can hang it up
85074.e: With the rope you can pull the person holding the ring to the shore or the boat. The ring then does not drift away.
85074.m: You pull the ring back with the rope.

85075.e: A lifebuoy is round with a hole in the middle. That way you can hold it well or slip into it.
85075.m: A lifebuoy is round with a hole.

a: It is made of very light material
85076.e: Lifebuoys are made of light foam, or in the past of cork. That is why they float and can carry a person.
85076.m: A lifebuoy is light and floats.

85077.q: What should you do if you see someone in trouble in the water?
85077.e: Children should not jump into the water themselves, because that is dangerous. Shout loudly for adults or dial the emergency number 112.
85077.m: If someone is in trouble in the water, get help at once.

85078.q: What is the emergency number for an ambulance in Switzerland?
85078.e: 144 calls the rescue service with the ambulance. 117 is the police and 118 the fire brigade.
85078.m: In Switzerland you reach the ambulance on 144.

85079.q: What can a submarine do that an ordinary boat cannot?
85079.e: A submarine is a boat that can travel under the sea. It can dive and move under water.

85080.q: What does a submarine take into its tanks to dive?
85080.e: The submarine fills its diving tanks with water. This makes it heavier and it sinks.
85080.m: A submarine dives by taking in water.

85081.q: What does a submarine use to push the water out of its tanks to come up?
85081.e: Compressed air forces the water out of the diving tanks. The submarine gets lighter and rises.
85081.m: With air in its tanks, the submarine surfaces.

85082.q: What do you use to look above the water from a submarine under the surface?
85082.e: A periscope is a long tube with mirrors. You can look over the water with it while the boat stays below.
85082.m: You look out of a submarine with a periscope.

85083.q: Which Swiss explorer dived to the deepest point of the ocean in 1960 in the bathyscaphe “Trieste”?
85083.e: Jacques Piccard dived into the Mariana Trench with Don Walsh in 1960. The craft had been developed by his father, Auguste Piccard.
85083.m: Jacques Piccard dived to the deepest point of the ocean.

85084.q: Which animal dives and comes up again a bit like a submarine, while breathing air?
85084.e: Whales live in the sea but breathe air. They dive and come back to the surface to breathe.
85084.m: Whales come up to breathe air.

85085.q: Why do submarines have very thick, strong walls?
a: Because the water presses hard at depth
Because it is hot under water
85085.e: The deeper you dive, the harder the water presses from all sides. Strong walls can withstand this pressure.
85085.m: Deep down, the water presses very hard.

85086.q: At the 1964 national exhibition in Lausanne, a tourist submarine took people diving. In which lake?
85086.e: Lausanne lies on Lake Geneva. The tourist submarine “Mésoscaphe” sailed there, and about 33,000 people dived into the depths in it.
85086.m: At Expo 64, a submarine sailed in Lake Geneva.

85087.q: Where do you wear armbands for swimming?
85087.e: Armbands are pulled over the upper arms. They keep the arms and body up in the water.
85087.m: You wear armbands on your upper arms.

85088.q: What are armbands usually filled with?
85088.e: You blow armbands up with air. The air gives buoyancy and keeps the child up.

85089.q: May a child with armbands go into deep water alone?
a: Yes, if the armbands are colourful
85089.e: Armbands can slip off or lose air. That is why young children must always be watched in the water.

85090.q: What happens if an armband has a hole?
a: The air escapes and it no longer holds you up
It gets heavier and holds you up better
85090.e: The air streams out through the hole. Without air, the armband gives no more buoyancy.
85090.m: An armband with a hole no longer holds you up.

85091.q: What are the aids called that help young children stay up in the water more easily?
85091.e: Armbands, swim belts and other swimming aids give extra buoyancy. But they do not replace learning to swim.

85092.q: What should you do before a child puts on armbands?
a: Check they are well blown up
85092.e: Only well inflated armbands hold you up properly. So you check first that there is enough air in them.
85092.m: Armbands must be well blown up.

85093.q: Which foam board helps you learn to swim?
85093.e: You hold on to the kickboard with your hands and practise kicking. The board floats because foam is light.
85093.m: You practise kicking with a kickboard.

85094.q: What is the goal when a child learns to swim?
a: To be able to swim without armbands
To stay only in the paddling pool
85094.e: Armbands only help at the start. In swimming lessons you learn to stay above water without aids.
85094.m: In time, you learn to swim without armbands.

85095.q: What happens to an inflated beach ball in the swimming pool?
85095.e: A beach ball is full of air and very light. That is why it floats on top of the water.
85095.m: A beach ball floats on the water.

85096.q: Why is it hard to push a big beach ball under water?
a: The water pushes it strongly upwards
85096.e: A big ball full of air is pushed strongly upwards by the water. This force is called buoyancy.
85096.m: A big beach ball has lots of buoyancy.

85097.q: What does a beach ball do if you let go of it under water?
a: It jumps out of the water
It rolls away to the side
85097.e: Buoyancy shoots the ball upwards. Often it even jumps out of the water.
85097.m: A beach ball shoots up when you let go.

85098.q: Why does a beach ball drift away easily on a lake?
85098.e: The ball is light and sits almost entirely above the water. That is why even a light wind can blow it away.
85098.m: Wind blows light balls away on the water.

85099.q: How far does a beach ball sink into the water?
85099.e: A beach ball is very light. It only needs to push aside a little water, so it only dips in a little way.
85099.m: A beach ball only dips in a little.

85100.q: What is the ball sport in a swimming pool where two teams throw the ball into goals?
85100.e: In water polo two teams swim in the pool and throw the ball into the other team's goal. You are not allowed to touch the bottom.
85100.m: Water polo is played swimming in the pool.

85101.q: Why should you not swim far out into a lake with a beach ball?
a: It is not a rescue aid
85101.e: A beach ball can slip away or be blown away by the wind. It is a toy and does not protect you from drowning.
85101.m: A beach ball is a toy, not a rescue aid.

85102.q: What happens to a beach ball if you let the air out?
85102.e: Without air, the ball loses its round shape. It goes floppy and can be folded up.
85102.m: Without air, a beach ball goes floppy.

85103.q: Why do divers often wear a belt with heavy weights?
a: So they can dive down more easily
85103.e: The diving suit contains lots of air and gives strong buoyancy. The lead weights balance this so the diver can go down.
85103.m: Lead weights help divers to dive down.

85104.q: What is the back part of a boat called?
85104.e: The back part of a boat is called the stern. The engine or the rudder is often there.
85104.m: The back of a boat is the stern.

85105.q: What is left in a bowl when salt water evaporates in the sun?
85105.e: When it evaporates, only the water goes into the air. The salt stays in the bowl as white crystals.
85105.m: When salt water evaporates, the salt stays behind.

85106.q: Can you see shooting stars in every season?
85106.e: Small particles from space hit the Earth every day. That is why you can see shooting stars on any clear night of the year.
85106.m: There are shooting stars all year round.

85107.q: How big are most of the particles that glow as shooting stars?
85107.e: Most shooting stars come from particles smaller than a grain of sand or a pebble. Because they are very fast, they still glow brightly.
85107.m: Even a grain of sand from space can glow as a shooting star.

85108.q: How long can you usually see a shooting star in the sky?
85108.e: A shooting star darts across the sky very quickly. It has usually disappeared again after about a second.
85108.m: A shooting star is usually over after one second.

85109.q: What may you do, according to an old custom, when you see a shooting star?
85109.e: Many people silently make a wish when they see a shooting star. That is an old custom.
85109.m: When you see a shooting star, you may make a wish.

85110.q: Where is the best place to see shooting stars?
a: In a dark place without lights
In the middle of a bright city
85110.e: Bright light from lamps outshines the faint shooting stars. In the countryside or the mountains the sky is much darker.
85110.m: Shooting stars are best seen in a dark place.

85111.q: What is a shooting star called in scientific language?
85111.e: Experts call the glowing trail in the sky a meteor. The particle itself is called a meteoroid.
85111.m: A shooting star is called a meteor in scientific language.

85112.q: Why does the particle of a shooting star glow?
a: It races into the air very fast
It is lit up by lamps
85112.e: The particle races into the Earth's atmosphere at enormous speed. The air in front of it is squashed and becomes very hot, so the particle glows and burns up.
85112.m: The air slows the particle down so much that it glows.

85113.q: Roughly how high above us do shooting stars light up?
a: As high as a church tower
85113.e: Shooting stars usually light up at a height of between about 80 and 120 kilometres. That is much higher than aeroplanes fly.
85113.m: Shooting stars glow about 100 kilometres above us.

85114.q: In which month can you see the Perseids especially well?
85114.e: The Perseids are a meteor shower. The most shooting stars appear around 12 August.

85115.e: Every year the Earth passes through a trail of dust in space. Then you can see lots of shooting stars, the Perseids.
85115.m: The Perseids are a meteor shower.

85116.q: Which constellation are the Perseids named after?
85116.e: The shooting stars seem to come from the direction of the constellation Perseus. That is why they are called the Perseids.
85116.m: The Perseids seem to come from the constellation Perseus.

85117.q: Where does the dust that the Perseids come from originate?
85117.e: A comet called Swift-Tuttle has lost dust along its path. The Earth flies through this dust trail every year in August.
85117.m: The Perseids come from the dust of a comet.

85118.q: What is an old name for the Perseids?
85118.e: Around 10 August is the feast day of St Lawrence. That is why the shooting stars are also called the Tears of St Lawrence.
85118.m: The Perseids are also called the Tears of St Lawrence.

85119.q: When in the night can you usually see the most Perseids?
a: In the second half of the night
85119.e: After midnight, the constellation Perseus is higher in the sky. Then you usually see more shooting stars.
85119.m: After midnight you usually see more Perseids.

85120.q: About how many Perseids can you see per hour on a good night in a dark place?
85120.e: On the best night, in a very dark place, you can count up to about 100 shooting stars in an hour. In a city you see far fewer.
85120.m: On a good Perseid night lots of shooting stars fall.

85121.q: What do you need to watch the Perseids?
85121.e: Shooting stars dart quickly across the whole sky. That is why they are best watched simply with the naked eye.
85121.m: You do not need a telescope for shooting stars.

a: A stone from space lying on Earth
85122.e: Some chunks from space do not burn up completely. What lands on the ground is called a meteorite.
85122.m: A meteorite is a stone from space on Earth.

85123.q: Which metal are many meteorites made of?
85123.e: There are stony meteorites and iron meteorites. Iron meteorites are very heavy and also contain some nickel.
85123.m: Many meteorites are made of iron.

85124.q: Where is the largest known meteorite in the world?
85124.e: The Hoba meteorite lies in Namibia. It is made of iron and weighs around 60 tonnes.
85124.m: The largest meteorite lies in Namibia.

85125.q: In which canton was the “Twannberg” iron meteorite found?
85125.e: Many pieces of an iron meteorite were found at the Twannberg above Lake Biel in the canton of Bern. It is the largest meteorite found in Switzerland so far.
85125.m: The Twannberg meteorite comes from the canton of Bern.

85126.q: Where are especially large numbers of meteorites found?
85126.e: Dark stones stand out clearly on the white ice of Antarctica. Researchers collect many meteorites there every year.
85126.m: Many meteorites are found in Antarctica.

85127.q: Roughly how old are most meteorites?
85127.e: Most meteorites are about 4.5 billion years old. They are as old as our solar system.
85127.m: Meteorites are as old as our solar system.

85128.q: How can you often recognise an iron meteorite?
a: It is very heavy for its size
85128.e: Iron meteorites are much heavier than a normal stone of the same size. A magnet often attracts them too.
85128.m: An iron meteorite is especially heavy.

85129.q: Which planet do some rare meteorites on Earth come from?
85129.e: Large impacts on Mars have hurled rocks into space. Some of them fell to Earth as meteorites much later.

85130.q: What is formed when a large chunk from space crashes into the ground?
85130.e: On impact a lot of rock is hurled away. What remains is a large round hole, an impact crater.
85130.m: A chunk from space leaves a crater.

85131.q: Why can you see only a few old impact craters on Earth?
a: Wind, water and plants wear them away
85131.e: Rain, rivers, wind and plants are constantly changing the Earth's surface. That is why old craters disappear over time.
85131.m: On Earth the weather wears away old craters.

85132.q: In which of Switzerland's neighbouring countries is the large Nördlinger Ries impact crater?
85132.e: The Nördlinger Ries is in Bavaria in Germany. The impact happened around 15 million years ago.
85132.m: The Nördlinger Ries is a crater in Germany.

85133.q: What lies in the middle of the Nördlinger Ries crater today?
85133.e: The town of Nördlingen lies in the crater. Many people live there, and you can see the crater rim as a ring of hills.
85133.m: There is a town in the Nördlinger Ries.

85134.q: What is the raised ring around a crater called?
85134.e: On impact, rock is pushed outwards. This creates a raised rim around the crater.
85134.m: A crater often has a raised rim.

85135.q: What shape is an impact crater usually, seen from above?
85135.e: Even if the chunk strikes at an angle, a round crater usually forms. The reason is the huge explosion on impact.

85136.q: Is an impact crater much bigger or smaller than the chunk that made it?
85136.e: A huge amount of force is released on impact. That is why a crater is much bigger than the chunk itself, often about ten to twenty times.
85136.m: A crater is much bigger than the chunk.

85137.q: What is the hill called that can form in the middle of large impact craters?
85137.e: In large impacts the ground in the middle springs back. This creates a hill there, called a central peak.
85137.m: There is often a central peak in the middle of large craters.

85138.q: Roughly how often does Halley's Comet come near the Earth?
85138.e: Halley's Comet circles the Sun once in about 75 to 76 years. So a person sees it at most once or twice in their life.
85138.m: Halley's Comet comes about every 76 years.

85139.q: When was Halley's Comet last close to the Sun?
85139.e: The comet was last visible in 1986. Space probes also flew to it at that time.
85139.m: Halley's Comet was last seen in 1986.

85140.q: In which year is Halley's Comet expected back?
85140.e: The comet takes around 75 to 76 years for one lap. So after 1986 it will come back around 2061.
85140.m: Halley's Comet will come back in 2061.

85141.q: What did Edmond Halley find out about the comet named after him?
a: That it is made of iron
That it will soon hit the Earth
That it is a small planet
85141.e: The English astronomer Edmond Halley calculated that the comet keeps coming back. That is why it bears his name.
85141.m: Halley's Comet is named after Edmond Halley.

85142.q: What was the name of the European space probe that flew past Halley's Comet in 1986?
85142.e: The Giotto probe flew very close past the comet's nucleus in March 1986. It took the first detailed pictures of the nucleus of a comet.
85142.m: The Giotto probe visited Halley's Comet.

85143.q: On which famous old embroidered cloth can you see Halley's Comet?
85143.e: The Bayeux Tapestry shows events from the year 1066. Halley's Comet is embroidered on it too.
85143.m: Halley's Comet can be seen on the Bayeux Tapestry.

85144.q: What can you see every year when the Earth flies through dust from Halley's Comet?
85144.e: The comet has spread dust along its path. In May and October the Earth passes through it, and then there are shooting stars.
85144.m: Dust from Halley's Comet brings us shooting stars.

85145.q: Roughly how long is the nucleus of Halley's Comet?
85145.e: The nucleus is about 15 kilometres long and 8 kilometres wide. It looks like a potato.
85145.m: The nucleus of Halley's Comet is about 15 kilometres long.

85146.q: Why can we see a comet's tail?
a: The Sun lights up gas and dust
It is full of tiny lamps
85146.e: Sunlight is reflected by the dust. The gas is excited by the Sun and glows by itself.
85146.m: The Sun makes a comet's tail glow.

85147.q: When does a comet get a long tail?
a: When it comes close to the Sun
When it is far from the Sun
85147.e: Near the Sun the comet gets warm. Ice turns to gas and carries dust with it, and this forms the tail.
85147.m: A comet gets a tail close to the Sun.

85148.q: How many tails can a comet have?
85148.e: Many comets have a dust tail and a gas tail. The two point in slightly different directions.
85148.m: A comet can have two tails.

85149.q: What is a comet often called because of what it is like?
85149.e: A comet is made of ice mixed with dust and rock. That is why it is called a dirty snowball.
85149.m: A comet is like a dirty snowball.

85150.q: How long can a comet's tail get?
a: As long as a football pitch
85150.e: Comet tails can be many millions of kilometres long. Even so, the gas in them is very thin.
85150.m: A comet's tail can be millions of kilometres long.

85151.q: What did the word “comet” originally mean?
85151.e: The word comes from Greek and means something like “long-haired”. The tail looks like flowing hair.

85152.q: What does a comet get when it comes close to the Sun?
85152.e: The Sun warms the comet. Ice turns into gas and dust comes loose. This forms a long glowing tail.
85152.m: Close to the Sun a comet gets a tail.

85153.q: In 1997 the comet Hale-Bopp could be seen for weeks without a telescope. What did it look like?
a: Like a bright star with a long tail
85153.e: Hale-Bopp shone very brightly in the evening sky in 1997. You could see a bright head and a long, glowing tail.
85153.m: Hale-Bopp was a bright comet with a long tail in 1997.

a: A flash of lightning in a storm
85154.e: A fireball is a very bright shooting star. It shines more brightly than all the planets and stars.
85154.m: A fireball is a very bright shooting star.

85155.q: Why is a fireball brighter than an ordinary shooting star?
a: It is closer to the Sun
85155.e: With a fireball, the chunk from space is bigger than a grain of sand. That is why it glows much more brightly.

85156.q: What can you sometimes also hear with a large fireball?
85156.e: Large fireballs are faster than sound. This sometimes creates a bang like thunder.
85156.m: A large fireball can make a bang.

85157.q: What damage did the fireball that exploded over the Russian city of Chelyabinsk in 2013 cause?
a: The shock wave broke many windows
It set off a huge tidal wave
It darkened the sky for months
85157.e: On 15 February 2013 a chunk exploded high above Chelyabinsk. The shock wave broke thousands of windows, and many people were injured by splinters of glass.
85157.m: In 2013 a fireball exploded over Chelyabinsk.

85158.q: What else is a very bright fireball that bursts apart called?
85158.e: Experts also call very bright fireballs bolides. Sometimes they burst into many pieces.
85158.m: A very bright fireball is also called a bolide.

85159.q: Can anything from a fireball fall to the ground?
a: No, it always burns up completely
85159.e: With large fireballs, not everything burns up. The remains can fall to Earth as meteorites.
85159.m: After a fireball, meteorites are sometimes found.

85160.q: What colour is a fireball often?
85160.e: Fireballs often glow greenish, yellow or orange. The colour depends on the substances in the chunk and in the air.

85161.q: What should you do if you have seen a fireball?
a: Call the fire brigade at once
85161.e: Researchers collect reports from many places. That way they can work out the flight path and perhaps find meteorites.
85161.m: You can report a fireball to an observatory.

85162.q: When did the great dinosaurs die out?
85162.e: The age of the great dinosaurs ended about 66 million years ago. There were no humans for a very long time after that.
85162.m: The dinosaurs died out about 66 million years ago.

85163.q: According to most researchers, what hit the Earth when the dinosaurs died out?
85163.e: A giant chunk from space struck the Earth. This changed the climate all over the world.
85163.m: An asteroid helped to wipe out the dinosaurs.

85164.q: In which present-day country is the great crater from the end of the age of the dinosaurs?
85164.e: The Chicxulub crater is on the Yucatán peninsula in Mexico. Today it is hidden under rock and sea.
85164.m: The crater from the end of the dinosaurs is in Mexico.

85165.q: Roughly how big was the asteroid that ended the age of the dinosaurs?
85165.e: The chunk was probably about 10 to 15 kilometres across. That is about as wide as a small town.
85165.m: The dinosaur asteroid was about 10 kilometres across.

85166.q: What darkened the sky for a long time after the impact?
85166.e: The impact and the fires sent huge amounts of dust and soot into the air. It became dark and cold, and many plants died.
85166.m: After the impact, dust darkened the sky.

85167.q: Which animals today are descended from dinosaurs?
85167.e: Some small feathered dinosaurs survived. They became the birds that live today.

85168.q: Which animals survived the end of the age of the dinosaurs and became more common afterwards?
85168.e: Small mammals could hide and needed little food. After the dinosaurs died out, they spread widely.
85168.m: Small mammals survived the end of the dinosaurs.

85169.q: Roughly how many of the animal species alive at that time died out?
85169.e: About three quarters of all animal and plant species disappeared at that time. Many species in the sea and on land died out.
85169.m: About three quarters of all species died out then.

85170.q: In which country is the Barringer Crater?
85170.e: The Barringer Crater is in the desert of Arizona in the USA. It is also called Meteor Crater.
85170.m: The Barringer Crater is in Arizona in the USA.

85171.q: Roughly how wide is the Barringer Crater?
85171.e: The crater is about 1.2 kilometres wide and about 170 metres deep. It is one of the best-preserved impact craters on Earth.
85171.m: The Barringer Crater is about a kilometre wide.

85172.q: Roughly how old is the Barringer Crater?
85172.e: The crater was formed about 50,000 years ago. Because it rains little in the desert, it is still well preserved.
85172.m: The Barringer Crater is about 50,000 years old.

85173.q: What kind of chunk from space made the Barringer Crater?
a: A lump of ice from a comet
85173.e: Many pieces of iron were found around the crater. The chunk was probably about 50 metres across.
85173.m: An iron meteorite made the Barringer Crater.

85174.q: What did Daniel Barringer, after whom the crater in Arizona is named, claim?
a: A chunk from space made the crater
A river dug out the crater
85174.e: Daniel Barringer was a geologist. He was one of the first to claim that the crater was formed by an impact.
85174.m: The Barringer Crater is named after Daniel Barringer.

85175.q: Who trained at the Barringer Crater for the journey to the Moon?
85175.e: The landscape in the crater is like the Moon. That is why astronauts from the Apollo missions trained there.
85175.m: Astronauts trained in the Barringer Crater for the Moon.

85176.q: How did some researchers once think the Barringer Crater was formed?
a: By an earthquake under the sea
85176.e: In the past, some people thought the crater was a volcanic crater. Only later was it proved that a chunk from space had struck.
85176.m: The Barringer Crater is not a volcanic crater.

85177.q: What other name is the Barringer Crater known by?
85177.e: It is usually called “Meteor Crater”. Today it is a popular place to visit, with a museum.
85177.m: The Barringer Crater is also called Meteor Crater.

a: A chunk of rock from space hits a planet
85178.e: In an asteroid impact, a chunk of rock from space crashes into a planet or moon. Large impacts are very rare.
85178.m: In an impact, a chunk from space strikes.

85179.q: Where in Russia did an explosion from space flatten huge forests in 1908?
85179.e: In 1908 a chunk exploded in the air over Tunguska. The shock wave knocked down millions of trees.
85179.m: In 1908 an explosion at Tunguska knocked down millions of trees.

85180.q: What is formed when a large chunk of rock from space crashes into the ground?
85180.e: On impact a lot of ground is hurled away. What remains is a round pit, a crater. You can see many craters on the Moon too.

85182.q: Why do researchers watch asteroids near the Earth?
85182.e: Researchers search the sky with telescopes. That way people know early on whether a chunk could come dangerously close to the Earth.
85182.m: Researchers look for dangerous asteroids early.

85183.q: Do large asteroids hit the Earth often?
85183.e: Small particles hit the Earth all the time. But large, dangerous asteroids strike only very rarely, often only once every many millions of years.
85183.m: Large asteroid impacts are very rare.

85184.q: What usually happens to small asteroids before they reach the ground?
a: They burn up in the air
85184.e: The atmosphere protects the Earth. Small chunks burn up in it before they reach the ground.
85184.m: The air protects the Earth from small chunks.

85185.q: What could an asteroid impact in the sea set off?
85185.e: A large impact in the sea would move huge masses of water. A tremendous wave could form, a tsunami.
85185.m: An impact in the sea can set off a giant wave.

85186.q: What are tiny particles floating through space called?
85186.e: Lots of tiny grains float in space. They are called space dust or cosmic dust.
85186.m: Tiny grains in space are called space dust.

85187.q: Does space dust fall on the Earth every day?
85187.e: Every day many tonnes of tiny grains of dust trickle down onto the Earth from space. But we do not notice them.
85187.m: Space dust falls on the Earth every day.

85188.q: Where have tiny grains from space been found?
85188.e: Researchers have discovered tiny grains from space in the dirt from gutters and rooftops. You need a microscope to see them.
85188.m: Tiny grains from space can be found on rooftops.

85189.q: What are tiny meteorites smaller than a millimetre called?
85189.e: Most particles from space are tiny. When they reach the ground, they are called micrometeorites.

85190.q: What were stars and planets formed from?
85190.e: There are huge clouds of gas and dust in space. Stars and planets formed from them.
85190.m: Stars and planets form from gas and dust.

85191.q: What did a space probe once bring back to Earth from a comet?
85191.e: The space probe Stardust flew close past a comet and caught tiny grains of dust. In 2006 a capsule with the dust landed on Earth.
85191.m: A space probe brought comet dust to Earth.

85192.q: What did the Stardust probe use to catch comet dust?
85192.e: Stardust used aerogel, an extremely light foam. The fast grains of dust got stuck in it.
85192.m: Stardust caught dust with a light foam.

85193.q: Where does a lot of the dust in the solar system come from?
85193.e: Comets lose dust when they come close to the Sun. Collisions between asteroids also produce dust.
85193.m: A lot of space dust comes from comets and asteroids.

85194.q: Where did the Rosetta space probe fly to?
85194.e: Rosetta flew through space for ten years. In 2014 it reached the comet Churyumov-Gerasimenko.

85195.q: What did the Rosetta space probe achieve for the very first time in 2014?
a: Placing a small lander on a comet
85195.e: In November 2014 Rosetta set down the small lander Philae on a comet. Nobody had managed that before.
85195.m: Rosetta was the first to set a lander down on a comet.

85196.q: What was the Philae lander the first to do in 2014?
85196.e: Philae was the first device to land gently on a comet. It bounced twice before coming to rest.
85196.m: Philae was the first to land on a comet.

85197.q: Which space organisation sent Rosetta into space?
85197.e: Rosetta was a mission of the European Space Agency ESA. Switzerland is a member of ESA.

85198.q: How long was the Rosetta space probe travelling before it reached its comet?
85198.e: Rosetta took off in 2004 and only reached its comet in 2014. On the way it flew past the Earth and Mars several times.
85198.m: Rosetta travelled for ten years to its comet.

85199.q: Which Swiss university built an important measuring instrument for Rosetta?
85199.e: Researchers at the University of Bern led the ROSINA instrument. It studied the gases around the comet.
85199.m: The University of Bern built an instrument for Rosetta.

85200.q: What is Rosetta's comet often called for short?
85200.e: The comet's real name is Churyumov-Gerasimenko. Because the name is so long, people often just say Chury.
85200.m: Rosetta's comet is called Chury for short.

85201.q: What happened to Rosetta at the end of the mission in 2016?
a: It slowly touched down on the comet
85201.e: In September 2016 the researchers let Rosetta sink slowly onto the comet. That was the end of the mission.
85201.m: Rosetta ended its mission on its comet in 2016.

85202.q: What shape is the comet Chury?
85202.e: The comet is made of two parts joined together. That is why it looks like a rubber duck.
85202.m: The comet Chury looks like a rubber duck.

85203.q: Why do you see fewer shooting stars on a night with a full moon?
a: The moonlight makes the sky bright
It always rains at full moon
85203.e: The bright full moon lights up the sky. Then you can no longer see faint shooting stars.
85203.m: At full moon you see fewer shooting stars.

85204.q: Which planet, with its many impact craters, looks almost like our Moon?
85204.e: Mercury has almost no atmosphere and no weather. That is why its many craters last a very long time.
85204.m: Mercury is covered in impact craters.

85205.q: What is the Rosetta space probe named after?
a: An old stone with writing on it
85205.e: The Rosetta Stone helped people to decipher ancient Egyptian writing. The probe was meant to help solve the mysteries of comets in the same way.
85205.m: Rosetta is named after the Rosetta Stone.

a: Small stones, humus, water and air
85206.e: Soil is a mixture. It contains broken-down rock, humus, water and lots of air in tiny spaces.
85206.m: Soil is a mixture of rock, humus, water and air.

85207.q: Which animal loosens garden soil especially well with its tunnels?
85207.e: Earthworms dig tunnels and mix the soil. This helps air and water reach the roots.

85208.q: Roughly how long does it take for one centimetre of new soil to form?
85208.e: Rock breaks down only very slowly, and plant remains need time to turn into humus. Nature often needs a hundred years or more for one centimetre of soil.

85209.q: What do plants need soil for?
85209.e: The roots hold the plant firmly in the soil. They also take up water and nutrients from it.
85209.m: Plants get water and nutrients from the soil.

85210.q: Are there many living things in a handful of garden soil?
a: Yes, millions of tiny living things
85210.e: Countless bacteria, fungi and small animals live in a handful of good soil. Most of them are so small that you cannot see them.
85210.m: Countless living things live in good soil.

85211.q: Which animal with digging paws lives almost always underground?
85211.e: The mole digs long tunnels with its broad front paws. It pushes the soil up as molehills.

85212.q: What protects the soil on a slope from being washed away by rain?
85212.e: Roots hold the soil in place like a net. Without plants, rain can easily wash the soil away.
85212.m: Roots hold the soil in place.

85213.e: Sandy soil is made of lots of small grains. It feels rough and grainy and hardly sticks together.

85214.e: Humus forms from rotted plants and animals. It is dark brown or almost black.

85215.e: Leaves, branches and dead animals are slowly broken down. They turn into dark, fertile humus.
85215.m: Humus forms from dead plants and animals.

85216.q: Who turns leaves and plant remains into humus?
a: Small soil creatures, fungi and bacteria
85216.e: Worms, woodlice, fungi and bacteria eat and break down the remains. They are called decomposers.
85216.m: Soil creatures, fungi and bacteria make humus.

85217.q: Where in the garden can you make humus yourself?
85217.e: On the compost, vegetable peelings and garden waste rot down. After a few months they become good compost.
85217.m: Humus forms on the compost heap.

85218.q: What does NOT belong on the compost heap?
85218.e: Plastic does not rot and never turns into humus. Plant remains such as peel, leaves and grass, on the other hand, break down well.
85218.m: Plastic does not belong on the compost.

85219.q: Why do plants grow well in soil rich in humus?
85219.e: Humus gives plants lots of nutrients. It also stores water like a sponge.

85220.q: What slowly turns into humus in the forest in autumn?
85220.e: The leaves fall onto the forest floor. Soil creatures break them down, and this makes new humus.

85221.q: What does good humus smell like?
85221.e: Good humus has a pleasant earthy smell, like the forest floor. The smell is made by tiny soil bacteria.
85221.m: Good humus smells like the forest floor.

85222.q: Which layer of soil is right at the top?
85222.e: Right at the top is the topsoil with lots of humus. Below it come the subsoil and the rock.
85222.m: The topsoil is right at the top.

85223.q: Why is the top layer of soil usually the darkest?
85223.e: Leaves and plant remains fall on the top. That is why the most dark humus forms there.
85223.m: The topsoil is dark because of the humus.

85224.q: What lies right at the bottom under the layers of soil?
85224.e: Under the soil is the rock that the soil once formed from. It is called parent rock.
85224.m: There is rock under the soil.

85225.q: What are the layers of soil called by experts?
85225.e: Experts call the individual layers of soil horizons. Together they make up the soil profile.
85225.m: The layers of soil are called horizons.

85226.q: How can you see the layers of soil well?
85226.e: In a deep pit you can see the wall from top to bottom. There you can make out the different coloured layers.
85226.m: You can see the soil layers in a pit.

85227.q: Where in the layers of soil do you find the most earthworms?
85227.e: Earthworms eat plant remains and humus. That is why most of them live in the upper layers, which are rich in humus.
85227.m: Most earthworms live near the top of the soil.

85228.q: What is the layer of soil between the topsoil and the rock called?
85228.e: Under the topsoil lies the subsoil. It is lighter because it contains less humus.
85228.m: Between the topsoil and the rock lies the subsoil.

85229.q: Which layer of soil is often removed first and kept when building?
85229.e: The valuable topsoil, rich in humus, is removed on building sites and stored. Later it can be used again for gardens and fields.

85230.q: What is the outermost layer of the Earth, the one we live on, called?
85230.e: We live on the Earth's crust. It is the thinnest of the Earth's three big layers.
85230.m: We live on the Earth's crust.

85231.q: What are the Earth's three big layers?
85231.e: On the outside is the crust, below it the mantle and right in the middle the core. That is how the Earth is built.
85231.m: The Earth has a crust, a mantle and a core.

85232.q: Which is much thicker, the Earth's mantle or the Earth's crust?
85232.e: The Earth's crust is only a few dozen kilometres thick. The mantle is many times thicker and makes up most of the Earth.
85232.m: The mantle is much thicker than the crust.

85233.q: Which fruit is the structure of the Earth often compared with?
85233.e: The thin skin is like the crust and the flesh is like the mantle. The stone in the middle is like the core.
85233.m: The Earth is built like a peach.

85234.q: What comes up from inside the Earth during a volcanic eruption?
85234.e: Deep down it is so hot that rock melts. During a volcanic eruption it comes to the surface as lava.
85234.m: Volcanoes bring melted rock up to the surface.

85235.q: Roughly how far is it from the Earth's surface to the centre of the Earth?
85235.e: The Earth's radius is about 6370 kilometres. That is how far it is to the centre of the Earth.
85235.m: It is about 6400 kilometres to the centre of the Earth.

85236.q: Roughly how deep is the deepest borehole in the world?
85236.e: In Russia, on the Kola Peninsula, a hole was drilled about 12 kilometres deep. That is only a tiny part of the way to the centre of the Earth.
85236.m: The deepest borehole is about 12 kilometres deep.

85237.q: Does it get warmer or colder the deeper you dig into the Earth?
85237.e: The deeper you go, the hotter it gets. In deep tunnels such as the Gotthard Base Tunnel, the rock was over 40 degrees.
85237.m: It is hot deep inside the Earth.

85238.q: What is the Earth's core mainly made of?
85238.e: The Earth's core is made mainly of the heavy metals iron and nickel. Heavy substances sank inwards when the Earth was forming.
85238.m: The Earth's core is made of iron and nickel.

85239.q: Roughly how hot is it in the Earth's core?
a: About as hot as the surface of the sun
About as warm as a bath
As warm as a summer's day
85239.e: In the Earth's core it is about 5000 to 6000 degrees. That is about as hot as the surface of the sun.
85239.m: The Earth's core is almost as hot as the surface of the sun.

85240.q: Is the Earth's outer core solid or liquid?
85240.e: The outer core is made of hot, liquid metal. It surrounds the solid inner core.
85240.m: The Earth's outer core is liquid.

85241.q: Roughly how deep down does the Earth's core begin?
85241.e: Under the crust lies the thick mantle. The Earth's core only begins at a depth of around 2900 kilometres.
85241.m: The Earth's core begins about 2900 kilometres down.

85242.q: What does the Earth's core produce that lines up a compass needle?
85242.e: The liquid metal in the outer core moves. This creates the magnetic field that the compass needle lines up with.
85242.m: The Earth's core makes the Earth's magnetic field.

85243.q: Has a person ever been to the Earth's core?
85243.e: The Earth's core is thousands of kilometres deep and far too hot. Scientists only learn about it through earthquake waves.
85243.m: No one has ever been to the Earth's core.

85244.q: How do scientists study the inside of the Earth?
85244.e: Earthquake waves travel through the whole Earth. The way they change tells scientists what the inside looks like.
85244.m: Earthquake waves reveal what the inside of the Earth looks like.

85245.q: Roughly how big is the Earth’s whole core?
a: About as big as the planet Mars
85245.e: The Earth’s core has a radius of about 3500 kilometres. That is roughly the size of the planet Mars.
85245.m: The Earth’s core is about the size of Mars.

a: A place where people dig valuable materials out of the ground
A railway station in the mountains
85246.e: In a mine, people dig for ore, coal or salt. The work often happens deep underground.
85246.m: In a mine, people take valuable materials out of the ground.

85247.q: What do you call a person who works in a mine?
85247.e: The workers in a mine are called miners. They dig out raw materials underground.

85248.q: What is a horizontal passage in a mine called?
85248.e: A mine tunnel (also called an adit) is an almost horizontal passage into the mountain. You can walk or ride through it into the mountain.
85248.m: A horizontal passage in a mine is a tunnel.

85249.q: Which bird used to warn miners about dangerous gas?
85249.e: Canaries react quickly to poisonous gas. If the bird became weak, the miners knew they had to get out.
85249.m: Canaries used to warn of gas in mines.

85250.q: Which greeting do German-speaking miners traditionally use?
85250.e: This is the old miners’ greeting. It wishes that you come back up to the surface safe and well.
85250.m: German-speaking miners have an old greeting that wishes them a safe return.

85251.q: What was mined in the Gonzen mine near Sargans?
85251.e: In the Gonzen in the canton of St Gallen, iron ore was mined for a long time. Today you can visit the closed mine.
85251.m: Iron ore was mined in the Gonzen.

85252.q: What do miners wear on their helmets so they can see in the dark tunnel?
85252.e: Underground it is pitch dark. A lamp on the helmet shines wherever the miner looks.
85252.m: Miners wear a lamp on their helmet.

85253.q: Which saint is the patron saint of miners?
85253.e: Saint Barbara is honoured by miners. Her feast day is 4 December.

85254.q: In which canton is the Bex salt mine?
85254.e: Bex lies in the Rhône valley in the canton of Vaud. There is a salt mine there that you can visit.
85254.m: The Bex salt mine is in the canton of Vaud.

85255.q: What is extracted from the mine at Bex?
85255.e: At Bex, salt has been taken out of the mountain for centuries. The salt comes from an ancient sea.

85256.q: How do visitors travel into the Bex salt mine?
85256.e: A small mine train takes visitors deep into the mountain. A tour then leads through old tunnels.
85256.m: At Bex you ride a little train into the mountain.

85257.q: Where are the passages of the Bex salt mine?
85257.e: The Bex salt mine lies inside a mountain in the Rhône valley. Many long passages lead deep inside.
85257.m: The passages at Bex are deep in the mountain.

85258.q: How did the salt in the mountain near Bex form?
85258.e: A very long time ago there was a shallow sea there. When the water evaporated, the salt was left behind.
85258.m: The salt at Bex comes from an ancient sea.

85259.q: Since when have people been digging tunnels into the mountain at Bex to get salt?
85259.e: The salt deposit was discovered in 1680. From 1684, tunnels were dug into the mountain.
85259.m: Salt has been mined at Bex for more than 300 years.

85260.q: What can you even find deep inside the mountain at the Bex salt mine?
85260.e: In one tunnel there is a restaurant for visitors. You can eat right in the middle of the mountain.
85260.m: There is a restaurant in the Bex salt mine.

85261.q: How is the salt at Bex taken out of the rock today?
a: It is dissolved out with water
It is melted out with fire
It is sieved out of the sand
It is scraped off with brushes
85261.e: Water is pumped into the mountain and the salt dissolves in it. Then the water is evaporated and the salt is left behind.
85261.m: At Bex, salt is dissolved out of the mountain with water.

85262.q: What is coal mainly burned for?
85262.e: When coal burns, it gives off a lot of heat. Power stations use it to make electricity.
85262.m: Coal is burned for heat and electricity.

85263.q: Which locomotives used to run on coal?
85263.e: In steam locomotives, coal heats up water. The steam drives the wheels.

85264.q: Which gas is produced when coal is burned and warms the climate?
85264.e: Burning coal produces a lot of carbon dioxide. This gas contributes to the warming of the Earth.

85265.q: Which kind of coal is younger and softer than hard coal?
85265.e: Brown coal (lignite) is younger and contains more water. Hard coal is older, harder and gives off more heat.
85265.m: Brown coal is younger than hard coal.

85266.q: What is a coal mine, for example in Germany’s Ruhr area, often called?
85266.e: A coal mine is often also called a colliery. In the past there were many collieries in Germany’s Ruhr area.
85266.m: A coal mine is called a colliery.

85267.q: What can you sometimes find as an imprint in pieces of coal?
85267.e: Because coal formed from plants, you sometimes find imprints of ferns and leaves in it. These are fossils.

85268.q: Roughly how fast does a layer of peat grow in a bog?
85268.e: Peat grows very slowly, about one millimetre a year. One metre of peat takes around a thousand years.
85268.m: Peat grows about one millimetre per year.

85269.q: What did people use dried peat for in the past?
85269.e: Peat was cut out and dried. Then it was burned in the stove to heat the house.
85269.m: Dried peat used to be burned for heating.

85270.q: Why do plants in a bog not rot away completely?
a: It is too wet and there is too little air
85270.e: In the wet bog there is no oxygen. So the decomposers cannot break the plants down completely, and peat forms.
85270.m: In the wet bog, peat is left over.

85271.q: Why should you use peat-free soil in the garden?
85271.e: To get peat, bogs are dug up, and they are home to many rare animals and plants. Bogs also store a lot of carbon.

85272.q: Are bogs protected in Switzerland today?
a: No, you may cut peat anywhere
85272.e: Since a popular vote in 1987, bogs in Switzerland have been protected. Peat may no longer be dug there.

85273.e: Peat is brown to blackish brown. You can often still see remains of moss and plants in it.

85274.q: What can peat turn into after a very long time deep in the ground?
85274.e: When peat is covered and pressed by many layers, it changes. After millions of years it can become brown coal and later hard coal.
85274.m: Peat can turn into coal after a long time.

85275.q: What is digging out peat called?
85275.e: In the past, people cut peat out of the bog in blocks with spades. This is called peat cutting.
85275.m: Digging out peat is called peat cutting.

a: From water that leaves behind limestone
85276.e: Water dissolves lime from the rock. When it drips down in the cave, a little lime is left behind and slowly turns to stone.
85276.m: Dripstones form from lime in water.

85277.q: In which canton are the Höllgrotten, a well-known dripstone cave?
85277.e: The Höllgrotten are near Baar in the canton of Zug. You can admire many beautiful dripstones there.
85277.m: The Höllgrotten are in the canton of Zug.

85278.q: What is the temperature like in a cave throughout the year?
85278.e: Deep in the mountain, you notice little of the weather outside. So caves stay about equally cool all year round.
85278.m: Caves are cool all year round.

85279.q: Why should you not touch dripstones?
a: Grease from your skin stops them growing
85279.e: The grease from your skin stays on the stone. No new lime can then build up there.

85280.q: Which animals often sleep in caves in winter?
85280.e: Bats hibernate in caves. It is quiet, dark and frost-free there.
85280.m: Bats often spend the winter in caves.

85281.q: In what kind of rock do dripstone caves usually form?
85281.e: Water can slowly dissolve limestone. This creates caves, and dripstones inside them.

85282.q: What do you call people who explore caves?
85282.e: Cavers climb and crawl through caves and draw maps of them. They wear a helmet and a lamp.

85283.q: What is best to wear when visiting a dripstone cave?
85283.e: Caves are cool and often damp. So you need a jacket and sturdy shoes even in summer.
85283.m: Take a jacket into a cave.

85284.q: What is a stalactite made of?
85284.e: A stalactite is a dripstone made of limestone. It forms drop by drop over a very long time.
85284.m: A stalactite is made of limestone.

85285.q: How fast does a stalactite usually grow?
85285.e: Stalactites often grow only about one centimetre in a hundred years. So large dripstones are very old.

85286.q: What shape does a stalactite usually have?
85286.e: A stalactite gets thinner and thinner towards the bottom. It looks like an icicle made of stone.
85286.m: A stalactite looks like an icicle.

85287.q: Where does a stalactite hang in a cave?
85287.e: A stalactite grows downwards from the ceiling. It hangs like a stone icicle.

85288.q: What forms when a stalactite and a stalagmite grow together?
85288.e: When a hanging and a standing dripstone grow together, a column forms. Experts call it a stalagnate.
85288.m: Dripstones that have grown together form a column.

85289.q: Why should you not touch dripstones in a cave?
a: They can break and hardly grow back
85289.e: Dripstones grow very slowly. If a piece breaks off or grease from your hands gets on it, it hardly grows any further there.

85290.q: What always hangs at the tip of a growing stalactite?
85290.e: At the tip, the lime-rich water gathers into a drop. Before it falls, it leaves a little lime behind.
85290.m: A drop hangs from a growing stalactite.

85291.q: Apart from caves, where can small stalactites sometimes form?
85291.e: Water can also dissolve lime out of concrete. So small lime icicles sometimes grow under bridges and in tunnels.
85291.m: Small stalactites also grow under concrete bridges.

85292.e: A stalagmite grows where the drops fall on the floor. It slowly grows upwards.
85292.m: A stalagmite grows from the floor upwards.

85293.q: Why is a stalagmite often right under a stalactite?
a: That is where the drops fall
85293.e: The drops fall from the tip of the stalactite onto the floor. Lime builds up exactly there, and a stalagmite grows.
85293.m: A stalagmite grows under the drip.

85294.q: What does the tip of a stalagmite usually look like?
85294.e: The drops splash and spread out. That is why stalagmites are usually thicker and rounder on top than stalactites.
85294.m: Stalagmites are usually round on top.

85295.q: Which is usually thicker, a stalagmite or a stalactite?
85295.e: When the drop lands, it splashes out widely. So the stalagmite on the floor usually becomes wider than the stalactite on the ceiling.
85295.m: Stalagmites are usually thicker than stalactites.

85296.q: What does a stalagmite need to be able to grow?
85296.e: Without dripping water containing lime, no stalagmite grows. It does not need sunlight, though.
85296.m: A stalagmite needs dripping water with lime.

85297.q: What is one word for both stalactites and stalagmites?
85297.e: Stalactites and stalagmites both form from dripping water. That is why together they are called dripstones.

85298.e: Stalagmites grow in caves where water containing lime drips from the ceiling.

85299.q: Can stalagmites grow several metres tall?
a: Yes, over a very long time
No, never taller than a finger
85299.e: Because they grow very slowly, tall stalagmites often need many thousands of years. Some are several metres tall.

85300.q: What is it called when rain or wind wears away the soil?
85300.e: Water and wind can carry away fertile soil. This process is called erosion.
85300.m: Wearing away of soil is called erosion.

85301.q: What is a vertical passage in a mine called?
85301.e: A shaft leads straight down into the depths. Lift cages carrying people and material travel up and down it.
85301.m: A vertical passage in a mine is a shaft.

85302.q: What do you call mining coal in a huge open pit?
85302.e: If the coal is not deep down, it is dug out in an open pit. This is called opencast mining, because people work under the open sky.
85302.m: Coal from open pits comes from opencast mining.

85303.q: What is the very long cave in the Muota valley in the canton of Schwyz called?
85303.e: The Hölloch in the Muota valley is more than 200 kilometres long. It is one of the longest caves in the world.
85303.m: The Hölloch in the Muota valley is one of the longest caves in the world.

85304.e: Recyclable materials are waste such as paper, glass or metal from which something new can be made. That is why they are collected separately.
85304.m: A recyclable material is waste that still has value.

85305.q: How do you hand in waste paper in many Swiss municipalities?
a: Tied in bundles for the paper collection
85305.e: In many municipalities, people tie waste paper with string and put it out by the road on collection day. That way it can be recycled.
85305.m: Waste paper is bundled and collected separately.

85306.q: Which symbol often stands for recycling?
85306.e: The recycling symbol is made of three arrows going round in a circle. It shows that a material goes back into the cycle.
85306.m: Three arrows in a circle stand for recycling.

85307.q: Which metal are many drinks cans made of?
85307.e: Many drinks cans are made of aluminium. Old aluminium can be melted down and made into new cans.
85307.m: Aluminium drinks cans go to the aluminium collection.

85308.q: What do you call a place where you can hand in glass, cans and used oil?
85308.e: At a collection point there are containers for different recyclable materials. Everything is collected separately there.
85308.m: At the collection point you hand in recyclables separately.

85309.q: Why are recyclable materials collected separately?
85309.e: New products are made from separately collected materials. That means fewer new raw materials have to be taken from nature.
85309.m: Recycling saves raw materials from nature.

85310.q: What goes in the cardboard collection?
85310.e: Cardboard is collected like paper and made into new cardboard. Yoghurt pots are made of plastic and do not belong there.
85310.m: Cardboard boxes go to the cardboard collection.

85311.q: What is a Brockenhaus in Switzerland?
85311.e: At a Brockenhaus, also called a Brocki, you can drop off and buy used furniture, clothes and crockery. That way things are used again instead of thrown away.
85311.m: At the Brocki, old things get a second life.

85312.q: Which colour should you put a blue glass bottle with?
85312.e: There is no separate container for blue or red glass. Other colours go with green glass, because green glass copes best with other colours.
85312.m: Coloured glass goes with green glass.

85313.q: What does NOT belong in the bottle bank?
85313.e: Only bottles and jars for food belong in the bottle bank. Mirrors, window glass or drinking glasses melt differently and spoil the recycling.
85313.m: Only bottles and food jars belong in the bottle bank.

85314.q: What do you do with the lid before putting a jar in the bottle bank?
85314.e: Lids are usually made of metal and do not belong with the glass. You take them off and put them in the metal collection.
85314.m: Take the lid off before recycling a jar.

85315.q: On which day are you usually not allowed to use bottle banks in Switzerland?
85315.e: Throwing glass in is noisy. That is why it is forbidden on Sundays and at night in most municipalities.
85315.m: On Sunday the bottle bank stays quiet.

85316.q: What is made from melted waste glass?
85316.e: Waste glass is crushed, melted and shaped into bottles and jars again. That uses less energy than making brand new glass.
85316.m: Old glass is made into new bottles.

85317.q: How often can glass be recycled?
85317.e: Glass does not lose its quality when it is melted down. That is why it can be made into new glass again and again.
85317.m: Glass can be recycled again and again.

85318.q: What is the most important raw material for glass?
85318.e: Glass is mainly made from quartz sand, which is melted at very high temperatures. Collecting waste glass saves sand and energy.
85318.m: Glass is mainly made from sand.

85319.q: What is a PET bottle made of?
85319.e: PET is a type of plastic. It is light and does not break easily.
85319.m: PET bottles are made of plastic.

85320.q: Where can you return empty PET drinks bottles in Switzerland?
a: In the PET collection box in shops
85320.e: Almost everywhere that sells drinks in PET bottles has a collection box. You can return the empty bottles there for free.
85320.m: You take empty PET bottles back to the shop.

85321.q: What goes in the PET collection?
85321.e: Only drinks bottles go in the PET collection. Other plastic packaging spoils the recycling.
85321.m: Only drinks bottles go in the PET collection.

85322.q: What do you do with an empty PET bottle before putting it in?
85322.e: Squashed bottles take up less space. More bottles fit in a collection bag and fewer journeys are needed.

85323.q: What are collected PET bottles often made into?
85323.e: The collected PET is cleaned, shredded and melted. New drinks bottles are made from it.
85323.m: Old PET bottles become new PET bottles.

85324.q: Apart from bottles, what can be made from recycled PET?
85324.e: PET can be spun into fine threads. These are used, for example, to make fleece fabric for jumpers and jackets.
85324.m: PET can also be made into fabric for clothes.

85325.q: Why is PET recycling good for the environment?
85325.e: New PET is made from crude oil. Recycling PET means less oil and less energy are needed.

85326.q: Why should a PET bottle never be left lying in nature?
85326.e: Plastic hardly breaks down in nature. A bottle thrown away stays there for a very long time and harms animals.
85326.m: Plastic in nature stays for a very long time.

85327.e: Plant waste such as fruit, vegetables and leaves goes on the compost. Over time it turns into new soil.
85327.m: Fruit and vegetable scraps go on the compost.

85328.e: Earthworms eat the plant waste and loosen everything up. Their droppings are a very good fertiliser.
85328.m: Earthworms are busy helpers in the compost.

85329.q: What does a compost heap turn into?
85329.e: In the compost, plant waste turns into dark, rich soil. You can use it to feed plants in the garden.

85330.q: What does NOT belong on the garden compost?
85330.e: Cooked food and meat attract rats and other animals. That is why they do not belong on the garden compost.
85330.m: Meat scraps do not belong on the compost.

85331.q: What is the collection of garden and kitchen waste called in Switzerland?
85331.e: Many municipalities collect green waste such as grass cuttings, branches and vegetable peelings. It is made into compost or biogas.
85331.m: Green waste is waste from the garden and kitchen.

85332.q: What do tiny fungi and bacteria do in the compost?
85332.e: Fungi and bacteria are so small you can hardly see them. They break the plant waste down into tiny pieces.
85332.m: Tiny living things break down the compost.

85333.q: What can be produced from green waste in a biogas plant?
85333.e: In a biogas plant, bacteria break down the green waste without air. This produces gas that can be used to make electricity and heat.
85333.m: Green waste can be made into biogas.

85334.q: How long does it take for garden waste to turn into compost?
85334.e: The living things in the compost work slowly. It usually takes several months to about a year until the compost is ready.
85334.m: Good compost needs a few months.

85335.q: What is the bag for normal household waste called in Switzerland?
85335.e: Waste that cannot be recycled goes in the rubbish bag. It is picked up by the rubbish collection.
85335.m: Household waste goes in the rubbish bag.

85336.q: Why do rubbish bags cost extra in many Swiss municipalities?
85336.e: If you make a lot of rubbish, you need more bags and pay more. This is meant to encourage people to avoid waste and separate recyclables.

85337.q: Where do the contents of the rubbish bag go in Switzerland?
85337.e: In Switzerland, the waste from rubbish bags is burnt in a waste incineration plant. It is called a KVA for short.

85338.q: What is produced when waste is burnt in an incineration plant?
85338.e: The heat from burning is put to use. It makes electricity and heats homes through pipes.
85338.m: Burning waste produces heat and electricity.

85339.q: Where does an empty metal tin go?
85339.e: Tins are made of sheet metal. Scrap metal can be melted down and used again.
85339.m: Metal tins go to the metal collection.

85340.q: Where should a pair of trousers in good condition that has become too small go?
85340.e: Good clothes can be put in collection bins or passed on. That way other people can still wear them.
85340.m: Good clothes go to the clothes collection.

85341.q: What helps most to avoid waste?
85341.e: A water bottle can be refilled many times. That means fewer disposable bottles and cups are needed.
85341.m: Reusing is better than throwing away.

85342.q: What is it called when you simply drop rubbish on the ground?
85342.e: Littering means carelessly leaving or throwing away rubbish. In many Swiss towns you can be fined for it.
85342.m: Rubbish belongs in the bin, not on the ground.

85343.q: Where do empty aluminium coffee capsules go?
a: To the aluminium or capsule collection
85343.e: Aluminium coffee capsules can be returned at collection points or in shops. The aluminium is recycled.

85344.q: Where do you take used batteries in Switzerland?
85344.e: In Switzerland, shops that sell batteries must take old batteries back. They have collection boxes.
85344.m: You take used batteries back to the shop.

85345.q: Why do batteries not belong in the rubbish bag?
85345.e: Batteries contain substances that can harm the environment. When recycled, they are handled safely.
85345.m: Batteries contain substances that must not get into the environment.

85346.q: How much does it cost to return old batteries to a shop?
85346.e: When you buy a battery, you already pay a small fee for recycling. That is why returning it is free.

a: A battery you can charge again
85347.e: A rechargeable battery can be charged again and again. When it no longer holds its charge, it goes to the collection point like a normal battery.
85347.m: A rechargeable battery is a battery you can recharge.

85348.q: Why are old lithium batteries dangerous in household rubbish?
85348.e: Damaged lithium batteries can get very hot and catch fire. That is why they belong in the battery collection.
85348.m: Lithium batteries can burn and belong at the collection point.

85349.q: What can be recovered from old batteries?
a: Metals such as zinc and iron
85349.e: In battery recycling the metals are separated. Zinc, iron and other metals can be used again.
85349.m: Metals are recovered from old batteries.

85350.q: Which symbol on batteries shows that they do not belong in the rubbish?
85350.e: The crossed-out wheelie bin means the item does not belong in normal rubbish. You find it on batteries and electrical devices.
85350.m: A crossed-out wheelie bin means it does not go in the rubbish.

85351.q: Why must button batteries be kept away from small children?
85351.e: Small children could swallow a button battery. That can cause serious injuries inside the body.
85351.m: Keep button batteries out of reach of small children.

85352.q: Which animals often mistake plastic bags in the sea for jellyfish?
85352.e: Sea turtles like to eat jellyfish. A plastic bag in the water looks similar and can make them ill.
85352.m: Plastic bags in the sea are dangerous for turtles.

85353.q: How does a lot of plastic waste get into the sea?
85353.e: Rubbish dropped on land often ends up in streams and rivers. They carry it all the way to the sea.
85353.m: Rivers carry rubbish all the way to the sea.

85354.q: What is a huge collection of plastic waste in the ocean called?
85354.e: Ocean currents turn in circles and collect rubbish there. This creates large garbage patches.
85354.m: Ocean currents gather plastic into garbage patches.

85355.q: In which ocean is the largest known garbage patch?
85355.e: The largest known garbage patch lies in the North Pacific between Hawaii and California. It is called the Great Pacific Garbage Patch.
85355.m: The largest garbage patch is in the Pacific.

85356.q: How long does a plastic bottle take to break down in the sea?
85356.e: In the sea, plastic breaks down only very slowly into smaller and smaller pieces. Experts estimate this can take hundreds of years.
85356.m: Plastic stays in the sea for hundreds of years.

85357.q: Why is plastic dangerous for seabirds?
85357.e: Seabirds think pieces of plastic are food and eat them. Their stomach is then full, but the bird gets no nourishment.
85357.m: Seabirds can die from swallowed plastic.

85358.q: What is a lost fishing net drifting in the sea called?
85358.e: Ghost nets drift ownerless in the sea. Fish, dolphins and turtles can get caught in them.
85358.m: Lost fishing nets are called ghost nets.

85359.q: Via which river can rubbish from Switzerland reach the North Sea?
85359.e: The Rhine flows from Switzerland through Germany and the Netherlands into the North Sea. Rubbish in the Rhine can reach the sea this way.
85359.m: The Rhine flows into the North Sea.

85360.e: Microplastics are very small pieces of plastic. They are found in water, in soil and in the air.
85360.m: Microplastics are tiny bits of plastic.

85361.q: Up to what size are bits of plastic called microplastic?
85361.e: Plastic pieces smaller than 5 millimetres are called microplastic. Many are so small you cannot see them.

85362.q: Where does a lot of microplastic in Switzerland come from?
85362.e: When driving, car tyres wear down on the road. The fine particles end up in soil and water.
85362.m: Car tyres lose tiny particles when driving.

85363.q: Which clothes lose a lot of microplastic when washed?
85363.e: Fleece is made of plastic fibres. When washed, tiny fibres come loose and end up in the waste water.
85363.m: Clothes made of synthetic fibres lose microplastic when washed.

85364.q: Where has microplastic already been found?
a: In the sea, in lakes and in soil
85364.e: Microplastic has spread almost everywhere. Researchers have found it in the sea, in Swiss lakes and even in snow.
85364.m: Microplastic is almost everywhere on Earth.

85365.q: What can you use to see very small microplastic?
85365.e: Many particles are smaller than a grain of sand. With a microscope you can see them magnified.
85365.m: Under a microscope you can see tiny bits of plastic.

85366.q: What happens to a plastic bag that lies in the sun and water for a long time?
85366.e: Sunlight and waves make plastic brittle. It breaks into smaller and smaller pieces but does not disappear.
85366.m: Big pieces of plastic break down into microplastic.

85367.q: What helps to make less microplastic in the washing machine?
a: Wearing clothes made of natural fibres
85367.e: Clothes made of cotton or wool are not made of plastic. They do not release microplastic when washed.
85367.m: Natural fibres do not release microplastic.

85368.q: What does a sewage treatment plant do?
85368.e: In the sewage treatment plant, dirty water from homes is cleaned. Afterwards it can flow back into nature.
85368.m: The sewage treatment plant makes dirty water clean.

85369.q: What is a sewage treatment plant often called for short in Switzerland?
85369.e: ARA stands for Abwasserreinigungsanlage, a waste water treatment plant. Almost every municipality in Switzerland is connected to an ARA.
85369.m: In Switzerland, the sewage treatment plant is called ARA.

85370.q: Where does the water from the toilet go?
85370.e: Waste water flows through pipes in the sewers to the sewage treatment plant. There it is cleaned.
85370.m: Waste water flows through the sewers to the treatment plant.

85371.q: Who helps to clean the water in a sewage treatment plant?
85371.e: In the aeration tank, bacteria eat the dirt in the water. This makes the water cleaner.
85371.m: Bacteria eat the dirt in waste water.

85372.q: What should you never throw down the toilet?
85372.e: Cotton buds, wet wipes and other rubbish block pipes and cause problems at the treatment plant. They belong in the rubbish bag.
85372.m: Only toilet paper goes down the toilet.

85373.q: Where does the cleaned water from the treatment plant go?
a: Straight into the drinking water pipes
85373.e: The cleaned water is let into a stream, river or lake. It is clean enough for nature, but it is not drinking water.
85373.m: Cleaned waste water flows back into nature.

85374.q: What happens to sewage sludge in Switzerland?
a: It is dumped in the sea
85374.e: Sewage sludge can contain harmful substances. That is why in Switzerland it may no longer be spread on fields and is burnt instead.
85374.m: Sewage sludge is burnt in Switzerland.

85375.q: What is the large tank in a treatment plant called where gas is made from sludge?
85375.e: In the digester tower, bacteria break down the sludge without air. The gas that forms is used for electricity and heat.
85375.m: In the digester tower, gas is made from sewage sludge.

85376.e: Hazardous waste contains poisonous or dangerous substances. It must be collected separately and treated specially.
85376.m: Dangerous waste is called hazardous waste.

85377.e: Paints and varnishes contain substances that pollute water and soil. That is why you take them to the hazardous waste collection.

85379.q: How can you recognise dangerous substances on packaging?
a: By a diamond with a red border
85379.e: Hazard symbols are black pictures in a diamond with a red border. They warn, for example, of fire or poison.
85379.m: A red diamond warns of danger.

85380.q: Where do spray cans that still have paint in them go?
85380.e: Spray cans with leftovers are under pressure and contain chemicals. That is why they count as hazardous waste.
85380.m: Spray cans that are not empty are hazardous waste.

85381.q: Where do you take a broken mobile phone?
85381.e: Shops that sell electrical devices take old devices back for free. The valuable metals are recycled.
85381.m: You return old electrical devices to the shop.

85382.q: Why do energy-saving light bulbs not belong in the rubbish?
a: They keep glowing in the bag
85382.e: Energy-saving bulbs contain a small amount of poisonous mercury. That is why you return them to a shop or collection point.
85382.m: Energy-saving bulbs go to the collection point.

a: Making something new out of something old
Throwing new things away at once
85383.e: With upcycling, an old object becomes something new and useful. That way it does not become rubbish.
85383.m: With upcycling, old things get a new purpose.

85384.q: What is an example of upcycling?
a: Using a jam jar as a vase
Putting a jar in the bottle bank
85384.e: An empty jam jar can be used as a flower vase. The jar keeps being used.
85384.m: An old jar can get a new job.

85385.q: What can you sew from an old pair of jeans?
85385.e: Denim is very strong. You can sew a bag or a pencil case from old jeans.
85385.m: You can sew bags from old clothes.

85386.q: What can you make from an empty tin?
85386.e: A clean tin without sharp edges can be painted. Then it becomes a holder for colouring pencils.
85386.m: An old tin can become a pencil holder.

85387.q: What can you build from old wooden pallets?
85387.e: Wooden pallets are used for transporting goods. You can build shelves, tables or sofas from old pallets.
